9836d857933786d3: Now that LLMs can help analyze commercial software binaries and recreate their functionality, one software developer and student has created a project designed to make this process more difficult.
Timo Zhang's project is called Blind LLM Agents (BLA), and as its name suggests, it attempts to interfere with efforts by AI agents to scrutinize app code.

"Coding agents can reverse-engineer shipped packages, CLIs, and WASM in minutes," Zhang told The Register in an email. "Classic obfuscation was built for humans and static tools, not LLMs that reason about meaning. Blind LLM Agents is a protection layer for that threat model."
Such agents can also help developers build alternatives to existing commercial software.

Last month, Artcraft, a two-person development shop, released seven open-source apps that aim to be replacements for Adobe's commercial apps Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Artcraft claims these apps are "clean-room reimplementations" written from scratch in Rust using Anthropic Opus 5.5.

Setting aside the question of whether enlisting an AI model to reimplement an app really immunizes the creator from legal risk, those making apps face the possibility that someone will have an LLM probe published app binaries and reconstruct them through reverse engineering. There's in fact a framework for this, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA).

Zhang has faced some criticism on social media for creating a limited barrier to copying other people's work (which at this point might simply be the work of another LLM). But not everyone accepts that all publicly accessible binaries should be easily available for review and reuse. BLA cannot prevent committed reverse engineering efforts, but it may add a bit of friction to the process when LLMs are involved.

"It doesn't write app code — it hardens what you've already built," Zhang said. "A transform pipeline (plus MCP tools / an agent Skill) applies renaming, lane splitting, seed-derived string encryption, build polymorphism, WASM export renaming, decoys, self-seal integrity checks, and a coverage matrix that won't claim protection it can't prove. Behavior stays equivalent; recovery cost goes up."
Zhang said various evaluations like red teaming and CrackMe challenges to recover keys or flags from hardened artifacts show that BLA is effective.

"We also drive REA (a reverse-engineering agent) against those builds," he said. "Fail-to-break is the pass. CI tracks defense score, self-verifies integrity coverage, and checks functional equivalence. We raise the cost — we don't claim it is unbreakable."

The project website says as much, noting that it raises the effort for analysis and adds decoy code, but doesn't promise protection against traditional interactive reverse engineering tools like Ghidra or Frida.

Zhang said he's aware of other software projects that aim to interfere with AI, such as Poison Fountain for poisoning training data and Anubis for deterring bots and scraping. BLA, he said, is different. It's for hardening shipping code against reverse engineering and LLM-aided analysis. ®

2dcde4b665668871: Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called "big math" is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means, and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World, by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend.

Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London's Millennium Bridge.

An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019).

a5443af359df1d11: They are learning how to be drivers of change locally
Originally published on Global Voices
Participants of the Voices of Democracy project in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photo by beYOUnd. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

The war in Ukraine has created a myriad of challenges for youth and their participation in public life and democratic processes, bringing displacement and misinformation as well as decreased opportunities for political engagement, economic activity, and access to information. At the same time, there are still avenues youth can pursue to contribute to political decisions and shape the fate of their communities.

Despite the war, people can still submit petitions, participate in public consultations, or advocate for their needs online, but there is a lack of awareness about such opportunities. Furthermore, vulnerable groups — including displaced persons, minorities, and rural communities — know they have a voice, but struggle to find it.

In 2026, the local non-governmental organization beYOUnd implemented a project to help youth from vulnerable groups acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to find their voices in this new era of digital democracy. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Yevheniia Holovenko, the chairwoman of beYOUnd, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Yevheniia Holovenko (YH): beYOUnd is a youth-led NGO based in Ukraine, registered in October 2025, though we’ve worked as a team long before that. Our mission is to increase the involvement of vulnerable youth, especially internally displaced people and young people facing difficult social and economic circumstances, in integration, self-realization, and civic life.

Our name reflects our philosophy: it starts with you; it goes beyond! Our team is largely made up of young people who’ve lived through the same challenges as the youth we work with, which shapes how we approach everything we do.

We joined the Digital Sparks initiative because digital democracy and civic space are exactly where Ukrainian youth need support right now. Safe, informed participation online is inseparable from resilience during war, and it matched our mission perfectly.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

YH: The war has pushed many young Ukrainians, especially internally displaced persons (IDPs), into digital spaces to stay connected, informed, and civically active, often without the tools to do so safely.
We saw a gap: young people were consuming information and even participating online, but without media literacy, digital security awareness, or confidence that their voice could shape anything.

We wanted to close this gap by developing practical digital safety and civic participation skills in displaced and marginalized youth. We wanted to give them an opportunity to share ideas on how to increase awareness of digital democracy with the involvement of young people in Ukraine.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
YH: Within the project “Voices of Democracy in the Digital Era,” we ran an awareness campaign covering digital security, e-participation, and disinformation, which reached over 8,500 views.
On the education side, we delivered three webinars and three workshops on digital democracy, media literacy, civic action planning, and cybersecurity, engaging over a hundred participants.

We also organized an offline networking event in the capital, Kyiv, bringing 27 participants together in person to connect around these same topics, and build on the online learning with real, face-to-face relationships and exchange.
Together, these activities, which combined online reach with in-person community building, gave young people both the knowledge and the network to act on this newly acquired knowledge.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

YH: “Voices of Democracy” reshaped how our beneficiaries see their own place in their community. As one participant shared, “I discovered new digital tools I can use to engage with my community and take part in important decisions.”
Others said the most valuable part was learning how to protect their personal data and use digital services safely in everyday life.
Several highlighted finally understanding the difference between advocacy and broader civic action, and how to build a real plan for their own initiative — skills that came alive through teamwork.

As another participant put it, “I learned to define a problem, trace its causes, and plan real steps to solve it — and I understood better what advocacy is and how it can drive positive change in a community.”
For many, this changed how they see their own ability to influence change locally.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

YH: Leading this project deepened our understanding of how closely digital safety and democratic participation are linked. You can’t meaningfully engage young people in civic life online without first equipping them to navigate that space securely.
Working alongside experts in digital security and civic engagement broadened our grasp of practical tools we now use, and how we think about beYOUnd’s programming.

It also pushed us to see capacity-building more structurally: not just what we teach beneficiaries, but how we build our own organizational resilience for the long term, not just on a project-by-project basis.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

YH: The biggest lesson was that combining practical, hands-on content with real interaction (webinars, workshops, and offline networking) worked far better than any one format alone. Participants didn’t just absorb information; they built relationships and confidence to act on it, especially through the in-person exchange in Kyiv.
We also learned how much value there is in simple, clear, practical content. Participants consistently said what stuck with them most was information they could immediately use, not abstract theory.
Finally, working through capacity-building for our own team alongside the project reminded us that organizational resilience matters just as much as the skills we pass on to beneficiaries.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

YH: We plan to keep the digital tools, advocacy frameworks, and civic action planning skills from this project embedded in how we design future programs for youth. This isn’t a one-off topic, but now a standing part of our work.
The connections built through the Kyiv networking event are something we want to keep nurturing, turning one-time contacts into an ongoing community.

On the organizational side, we’re applying what we’ve built around resilience and long-term capacity to strengthen beYOUnd as we grow, so we’re better equipped to run projects like this and bigger ones going forward.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

325f87658a3140c6: Google has announced a "super network" upgrade for its Fi cell service. For the past few years, Google Fi has operated exclusively on the T-Mobile network, but now it's adding support for a second 5G network. Oddly, Google refuses to say which one.

Google's MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) launched in 2015 as Project Fi with support for both T-Mobile and Sprint service. The service initially only worked on Google's Nexus phones, which would switch between networks based on signal strength. After T-Mobile absorbed Sprint, Fi switched to being a single-network service in the US while continuing to hop between networks for international travel.

With the super network, Google Fi is again a dual-carrier service stateside. Phones connected to Fi will be able to hop between T-Mobile 5G and a different 5G network to provide the best possible connectivity. Google's blog post announcing the change conspicuously doesn't mention either network, saying only that it supports "two of America’s best 5G cellular networks."

26bfbb0edd8801ac: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security Gateway (ESG) products that, when chained, could allow the crims to run commands with root privileges.
“We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations,” the security vendor said in a late Monday night update to its earlier security advisory.

Barracuda declined to answer The Register’s questions, including one about how many organizations have been hit by attackers. A company spokesperson told us that it “worked directly” with the affected businesses “to quickly address the issue. Barracuda acted promptly to remediate the vulnerabilities, releasing patches for affected products.”
The vendor disclosed and fixed the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, last week.

CVE-2026-116606 is a 9.3 CVSS-rated, pre-authentication authorization bypass flaw in ESG. While authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have access to the administrative user interface.
As Purplecop Security founder Tausif Ahmed said on Tuesday: “If your Email Security Gateway's admin UI is open to the internet, that's the first thing I'd close today.”

CVE-2026-111560 is an 8.6-rated command-injection flaw that affects multiple Barracuda products: its ESG, load balancer (ADC), message archiver (BMA), web application firewall (WAF), WAF control center (WCC), and web security gateway (WSG).

“If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda warned on November 2. At the time, the vendor did not report any active exploitation of either.

We don’t yet know who is responsible for the attacks, or whether the intruders gained root access – but if they did, they could steal data, install backdoors, and take full control of affected systems.

These types of edge-device exploits have been used by Chinese-government spies, and in 2023 the FBI blamed PRC-linked attackers for a series of attacks that targeted Barracuda ESGs to deploy custom malware and maintain access to high-value networks. According to Mandiant, 27 percent of identified affected organizations were government entities.
So if you haven’t already: patch now. ®

f3f225b501e14478: Built by a 14-year-old developer, a new tool called Autark treats AI agents as a virtual team that can work without constant prompting.
Users put tasks in an inbox, where a manager agent delegates them to other agents that carry out the work and report their results. Agents can also ask clarifying questions if tasks are too vague.
“Agents do not wait for a prompt,” Autark’s website explains. “A schedule, a timer, a new task, a message or an event wakes them up. They decide what to do, do it, and can plan their own next step.”

As one would hope from a product like this, Autark is model agnostic and can be set up to connect to OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code through those services’ CLI tools. Local models are also supported. Your mileage may vary if you choose to use anything besides Codex or Claude Code, though, as Autark’s website mentions support for other models is built in but hasn’t been tested in a live run yet, as Autark is still under active development as an open-source tool.

Autark is the brainchild of teenage Austrian developer Stanislaus Hees. He’s still in school, and tells The Register he’s deeply interested in AI and came up with Autark after being unhappy with existing AI tools.

“I could get help with individual tasks, but I still had to organise the work, remember what was unfinished and keep pushing it forward,” Hees said of his time using Claude Code and Codex. “I wanted a system that could take responsibility for ongoing work, not just respond to my next message.”

He developed Autark - or, more accurately, prompted AI coding tools to do it for him - to come up with a tool that could fulfill that want. You know what that means: It’s capable, but that capability also makes it dangerous.
Autark’s page on access and data makes clear what’s at risk if you give it unfettered access to a PC, and why you don’t want to let the thing run roughshod over a system.
“It can do everything,” the page explains, because “Autark does not put walls around its agents.”

There’s no sandboxing in Autark, no approval prompts, and no permission gates. It doesn’t stop agents from spending all the money they can get their hands on, deleting files, or sending unsolicited emails, either. Agents run with the privileges of the machine's user, with approval checks and permission restrictions disabled or bypassed. Even the safety limit parley that users have with Autark establishes guidelines, not rules.
“The first thing the AI asks is how far it may go,” the access page points out. “That is a question, not a technical barrier.”

That means agents given a task that conflicts with their stated limits may still attempt to carry it out. As we’ve seen in recent months, some AI agents have found ways around restrictions, instructions be damned.

“In our own live test runs, agents given a vague request reached real repositories, backups, SSH keys and .env files within minutes, and one changed the permissions of a file it had found,” the access page notes.
In other words, it’s probably best to stick Autark on a machine that doesn’t contain anything you’d want to avoid losing - even Hees admits as much.
“I would not claim that … the app is suitable for unattended access to sensitive systems,” the teen dev told us.

That’s not to say Autark lacks protections for secrets, though. Autark’s site explains that stored passwords and keys are encrypted and referred to using IDs that keep their values out of prompts. It also says its servers don't store user data, with a meeting server used to relay encrypted traffic between devices.

If you're willing to try Autark to see whether it can improve your workflows, you don't need to rely on its servers. While prepackaged apps are available from Autark’s website, it’s also fully open source and available on GitHub. Everything, even the meeting server code, is available for self-hosting and modification under an Apache open source license.

The bottom line is that this is a tool built by an ambitious young person, and it’s a tool with a lot of potential if used correctly. That correct usage is the major challenge, though, so be sure to build your own guardrails. ®
03e0860e077ac564: The Mozilla-backed Thunderbird project is getting closer to a wider launch of a hosted email service designed to complement its desktop mail app.

Now known as Thundermail (what else?), the service was originally developed under the Thunderbird Pro banner, which encompassed paid email, appointment scheduling, and file-sharing services designed to generate additional revenue for the organization.
The org has been inviting people from its Thundermail waitlist to try the service through an early-access program, and this writer just happened to be among them.

Thundermail offers a web-based email interface and can also be accessed through the Thunderbird desktop app, the Thunderbird mobile app for Android, or other compatible email clients. The Thunderbird apps remain free.

Users get an inbox with up to 15 email addresses and three custom domains, plus 30 GB of mail storage and 60 GB of send storage for Thunderbird Send, an end-to-end encrypted file-sharing and large-attachment service. That’s for starters – the org intends to offer those extra features and services at different price points.

Yes, Thundermail is a paid service, which may put off some users who are used to free email accounts offered via Gmail, Outlook.com and Proton Mail, but with the first two of those you do get served ads along with your messages.
The sign-up screens for Thundermail suggest the basic service will cost $6 per month, billed annually. This is roughly equivalent to the £55 we paid for a year on the early access program.

We asked Thunderbird when we can expect to see Thundermail officially launched and open to all comers. We will update if we get an answer. It previously said that a full launch is expected sometime in 2026.

The web-based user interface of Thundermail presents a fairly clean and uncluttered look, and could be likened to Gmail with the screen partitioned into a pane with folders on the left and a larger one to the right displaying messages.

A welcome screen introduces you to the features of Thundermail, which include the ability to work on several drafts at once, schedule delivery times for emails, create folders to arrange messages, contact lists and identities – all pretty much standard for an email system.

Firefox and the Thunderbird mail client both recently moved to a fortnightly release schedule in line with Mozilla’s plans, and Thunderbird itself gained support for Microsoft’s Exchange late last year. ®

6d2024e7c9bff0ed: After teasing its 256-core Epycs for more than a year, AMD is finally ready to talk about architectural changes to the Zen core that not only make it possible, but will eventually power its next generation of Ryzen processors in desktop and mobile PCs.

During a press event in Las Vegas last week, AMD spilled the beans on its latest Zen cores, which promise an average 27 percent uplift in instructions per clock (IPC) across a variety of AI and server workloads, along with boosted clocks ranging from 4.1 to 5.3 GHz. We expect to see even higher frequencies on consumer chips before long, but AMD isn’t quite ready to talk about Ryzen just yet.
CPU performance is a function of power, IPC, and clocks, and with gains across all three, the cores are shaping up to be one of the company’s biggest generational jumps ever.
A tale of two cores
As in past Epyc launches, Zen 6 isn’t one core. It comes in two flavors: a frequency-optimized variant (Zen 6) and a density-optimized version (Zen 6c).

This split dates back to the launch of AMD’s Bergamo Epycs in 2023, which packed 128 compact Zen 4c cores into just eight chiplets. The chip’s debut drew comparisons to Intel’s still relatively new Efficient (E-cores) for obvious reasons. But under the hood, AMD’s Zen 4c was nothing like what Intel was doing. The core itself was nearly identical to Zen 4; it simply traded clocks and a bit of cache per core for a more densely packed CPU die.
The only difference between running an application on Bergamo or Genoa was how quickly it executed. The same could not be said of Intel’s P and E cores, which used different ISAs.

This remained a defining characteristic and advantage of AMD’s compact core architecture through Zen 5, which allowed it to ship Turin parts with up to 192 cores without users having to worry about whether their app was running on a compact core or not.

With Zen 6c, at least as we understand it, this philosophy is largely unchanged. Both Zen 6 and Zen 6c share the same ISA, with clock being the main differentiator. There are other micro-architectural differences between the two cores designed to balance IPC and clock speeds more effectively.
Looking at the core’s block diagram, this isn’t immediately obvious. Zen 6 and Zen 5 share a very similar front and backend.

We'd be tempted to call the core iterative if it weren't for the 20 to 31 percent IPC uplift for cloud and AI workloads that AMD claims over Zen 5. This suggests that core for core, a 4.1 GHz Zen 6c-based Venice Epyc should deliver performance on par with a Zen 5-based Turin Epyc running at 5 GHz.

That's a pretty sizable jump, but just because AMD is seeing generational performance uplift in enterprise server and cloud workloads doesn't mean we'll see the same gains on the client side. Many will recall the roughly 5 percent performance gains gaming PC enthusiasts reported with the Ryzen 9000-series, leading to the rather unfortunate turn of phrase "Zen 5 percent."

That happened because game engines at the time simply weren't CPU-bottlenecked, and so faster cores could only raise the ceiling so much. Even so, AMD fellow and "Zen daddy" Mike Clark tells El Reg that PC buyers expect more than a 6 percent gain from Zen 6.

We're glossing over a bunch of low-level architectural optimizations here, but according to Clark, one of the biggest drivers of performance was the front end. Zen 5 introduced a dual front end, which for simple workloads worked great, but lost a lot of steam when confronted with more dynamic loads.

"The Zen 6 team did a really good job for those larger footprint workloads that have a bipolar nature," Clark said. "It's not something that comes through. You're not going to see it in a block diagram very well. It's sort of subtle... but it's a big lever."

Another contributor was the move to a distributed scheduler in the out-of-order pipeline. One of the biggest performance drivers in modern CPU cores is that they don't execute instructions in the order they receive them. Instead, they reorder the instructions so as to keep the core's backend execution units fed with a constant stream of instructions.

This is where we see the biggest difference between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. To account for the slower clocks on the latter core, AMD gave the core's scheduler deeper queues, which Clark tells us helps with higher-latency workloads. Meanwhile, from what we understand, Zen 6's shallower queue enables it to clock higher on less power.

Finally, on the backend, AMD made several subtle changes which should have major implications for vector heavy workloads, including AI. One of the more significant was the ability to perform four AVX2 or two AVX-512 loads per cycle.

While this doesn't improve AVX-512 performance much, for applications that haven't been updated to use it, the core is now able to perform twice as many loads, which should improve throughput for legacy applications. This should come in handy, particularly on PCs, where Intel's outright lack of AVX-512 support has made AVX2 the lowest common denominator for a lot of software.

That's not to say AVX-512 didn't get some love this generation. For those running AI workloads on CPUs, Zen 6 now natively supports FP16 datatypes. Previously FP16 was supported, but required padding the data to FP32, which meant the lower precision didn't buy much in terms of performance. That's no longer the case in Zen 6.
And while we're on the topic of AI acceleration, Clark notes that Zen 6 doubled the VNNI-INT8 pipes from two to four, and should effectively double throughput for workloads that support it.
Feeding the beast
While not strictly part of the core, AMD's Zen 6 processors also address one of the biggest asymmetries associated with its frequency and density optimized cores.

Going back to Bergamo, opting for a density-optimized Epyc didn't just come at the expense of clocks, but cache too. Each Zen 4c or Zen 5c chiplet contained twice as many cores, but the same amount of L3 cache.

With Zen 6 and Zen 6c, you may be giving up some clocks, but cache per core is now a constant 4 MB. As we discussed in a Venice deep dive back in September, each of the processor's eight CPU dies contains 12 or 32 cores and 48 and 128 MB respectively.

The benefit here is that users don't have to worry about different ISAs or cache hierarchies when optimizing their software stacks against AMD's Epyc processors. The same cannot be said of Intel's Xeon processors.

As we alluded to earlier, Chipzilla's performance and efficiency cores use different micro-architectures, ISAs, cache hierarchies, clocks, and even cluster their cores differently. This can pose real headaches if you have workloads that take advantage of fat vector registers like AVX-512, or accelerators like AMX, which will work just fine on Intel's P-cores but won't even run on their E-cores.
This, along with support for SMT (Hyperthreading), which Intel has dropped for now, could help the House of Zen vacuum up even more market share from its long-time rival. ®

d1ea4aef74f3bde9: AMD's cache-packed Epyc X chips are officially making a comeback.

Based on the House of Zen's frequency-optimized SKUs we looked at back in September, its HPC-optimized Venice-X parts will offer up to 96 cores and use the company's 3D V-Cache chip stack tech to triple the L3 cache density to more than a gigabyte.
But before you get too excited about another cache-packed Epyc, it'll be a little while before they actually ship. AMD expects the Venice-X to begin trickling out in the second half of 2027.

First teased at CES earlier this year, the chips are primarily aimed at latency-sensitive technical and scientific computing workloads like computational fluid dynamics and electronic design automation (EDA).

AMD itself relies heavily on its X-series Epycs for EDA workloads like functional verification testing, which is used to simulate silicon in order to ensure it behaves as it's intended to. According to AMD Fellow Phil Steinke, by keeping more of the model in cache, the CPU cores don't have to wait as long for data to move in and out of system memory.

Normally, boosting L3 capacity would have required larger chiplets with lower yields, but that's not how AMD has gone about it for the past four years. Instead, it used advanced packaging to give its existing CPU dies a little SRAM backpack.

This tech has been around for several generations now, having first debuted in the Ryzen 7 5800X3D back in 2022. That consumer desktop chip stacked a 64 MB SRAM tile on top of an 8-core chiplet, boosting L3 capacity to 96 MB. The extra cache made the chip one of the most potent gaming CPUs of the time.

Later that year, AMD brought the same technology to its Milan generation of Epycs as the company expanded its portfolio to address a wider range of workloads. The extra cache was popular enough to justify a second generation of X-series Epycs, which launched in 2023.
But then, nothing. When AMD unveiled its 5th-gen Epycs in late 2024, there was no Turin-X on the roadmap.

According to Madhu Rangarajan, who runs AMD's compute and enterprise AI products biz, this was intentional. "We are not doing the X every generation.... The enterprise HPC kind of market tends to have a cadence that's a little bit slower, so that's what drives our cadence."

Venice-X marks the return of AMD's X-chips, and for the most part, the processor largely follows the same recipe as its predecessors. Each of the chip's up to eight CPU dies is now bonded to a 96 MB SRAM tile using advanced packaging, for a total of 144 MB of L3 per chiplet or 1,152 MB per socket, which you might have noticed is the same as in the Genoa-X parts they replace.
But while core count and cache capacity haven't increased, clock speeds certainly have, with Venice now hitting 5.3 GHz compared to Genoa-X at just 3.7 GHz.
"In Milan and Genoa, there was one trade-off. You either had to choose something that was high frequency or you chose something with 3D V-Cache." HPC likes both, Rangarajan told El Reg.
The method for integrating the SRAM tile required this kind of compromise. Stacking SRAM on top of the compute chiplets boosted L3 caches, but also trapped heat, which limited boost clocks.

So, for the Zen 5 generation, AMD moved the SRAM tile from the top of the stack to the bottom. With the SRAM tile no longer acting as a blanket, the chips could run hotter and faster for longer. But while gamers enjoyed the higher clocks and bigger caches on AMD's Ryzen 9000 processors, only now with Venice-X are those improvements making their way into Epyc.

Because customers no longer have to choose between big caches and fast clocks, Rangarajan believes the chip may see wider adoption. "I think it's going to end up being much bigger in HPC than the previous generations where we had to make that tradeoff."

Curiously, if frequency weren't such a high priority, Venice-X may not have needed 3D stacked SRAM in the first place. As we reported earlier this year, AMD's top-specced Venice CPUs boast 256 cores and 1,024 MB of L3 cache.

AMD could have just fused off 160 of the cores and achieved a similar cache-per-core ratio. In fact, AMD did something like this for the Turin generation: For the Epyc 9175F, AMD essentially took a 128-core part and fused off 112 of the cores. What was left was a 16-core part with 512 MB of last-level cache.
"You could do that [with Venice], but then you don't get the frequency part of it. The Fmax would be at 4.1 gigahertz and not 5.3 GHz," Rangarajan said.
"Venice X really changes the game," he added. "For the first time, you can get the larger L3 in our highest frequency part." ®

afb491d043738fed: AMD's upcoming Verano processors aren't like any Epyc CPUs we've seen before. Rather than general-purpose workloads, Verano is designed specifically to power AMD's next generation of GPU servers.

In an interview with The Register during a press event in Las Vegas last week, Madhu Rangarajan, corporate VP of AMD's compute and enterprise AI products business, described Verano as being the first step towards building something that more closely resembles Nvidia's Vera Rubin superchips.

"Verano is really designed for an integrated CPU+GPU rack scale solution," he said. "From that perspective, I wouldn't say the CPU is a competitor to Vera. In a head note, I'd say the Verano+GPU solution is a competitor to Vera+Rubin."

For reference, Vera Rubin and the GB200 and GB300 that came before it aren't your typical server platforms. Instead they're more like an enormous single-board computer combining CPUs and GPUs into a tightly-integrated package. Each of Nvidia's superchips joins a single 88-core Vera CPU and 1.5 TB of LPDDR5X memory to a pair of Rubin GPUs via Nvidia's speedy NVLink-C2C interconnect.

Rangarajan tells us Verano will be the host CPU for a similar class of product using AMD GPUs, and much like Nvidia's superchips, the CPU will also use notebook memory rather than conventional RDIMMS.
However, unlike Vera, which is also being deployed as a standalone CPU in storage servers and agent sandboxes, Verano has a singular purpose: keeping its GPUs fed. (We assume they'll be MI500X GPUs.)

This design choice reflects AMD's philosophy of one SKU per workload. As such, Verano's core count, clock speeds, memory bandwidth, power, and I/O have been rebalanced to keep its GPUs fed and not much else.
Under the hood

If we were to peel back Verano's heat spreader, the chip looks a lot like the Venice Epycs we looked at back in September. It features either six of AMD's core complex dies (CCDs) for a total of 72 high-frequency cores clocking to 5.3 GHz, or 192 density-optimized cores clocking to 4.1 GHz, depending on whether the customer's workloads prefer core density or faster clocks.

But that's about where the visual similarities end. Much of the chip has been reworked to eliminate data flow bottlenecks between the CPU and the GPUs it is responsible for feeding. The chip features an entirely custom pair of I/O dies through which four LPDDR5X memory controllers are attached.

Those memory controllers are currently being validated for use with 24 channels of memory at up to 8,533 MT/s. We're told that we may see that creep up a bit depending on how much headroom AMD has when the part starts shipping next year, but for now that's what AMD is validating against.

That means the platform not only has fewer cores, but also slower memory. Peak theoretical memory bandwidth tops out at around 800 GB/s, which you might have noticed is half of what AMD's top-specced Venice parts can do and about 66 percent of Nvidia's Vera.

What LPDDR seems to buy AMD is a 30 to 40 percent reduction in power consumption compared to RDIMMS, as well as a more compact footprint for liquid cooling. But it also comes with some downsides. In its first incarnation, Verano won't be socketed. Instead it'll use a ball-grid array (BGA) that's soldered to the board, which will make it harder to service.

"LPDDR tends to be quite finicky in terms of speeds. Every time you go through a connector, you tend to lose a pin or two, and you already have one connector with the SoCam itself. So to minimize any of those losses in speed, we went BGA on the CPU," Rangarajan told us.
Unlike with a lot of notebooks, the memory itself won't be soldered down and will use the same SOCAMM2 modules found in Nvidia's Vera-Rubin and Vera-Vera CPU Superchips.
Even so, Verano looks like a bit of a downgrade compared to Venice except when it comes to CPU-to-GPU connectivity.
Fatter pipes

Historically, AMD's CPU-to-GPU communication has been done over PCIe. It works but has usually required PCIe switches to keep up with all the GPUs, NICs, and storage on board. Nvidia's superchip dispensed with this, replacing PCIe with its NVLink-C2C interconnect, which provides 900 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth to each of the system's GPUs.

Venice and Verano do something similar. Unlike past Instinct accelerators, AMD's latest generation of GPUs aren't limited to PCIe for CPU-to-GPU communication. Instead, starting with Venice, AMD transitioned to using xGMI.
Global memory interconnect (GMI) is how AMD has moved data between chiplets on its CPUs, GPUs, and APUs for several generations now. xGMI extends this to GPU-to-GPU and CPU-to-GPU communications.

With Venice, xGMI link bandwidth tops out at 64 Gbps per lane, which the keen-eyed among you have probably already figured out is the same as PCIe 6.0. Verano takes this to another level. As we mentioned earlier, Verano disaggregated the memory controllers, and AMD appears to have reclaimed that space for fatter Serializer/Deserializer (SerDes). Instead of 64 Gbps per lane, Verano's xGMI links top out at 112 Gbps, effectively giving it near PCIe 7.0 levels of bandwidth years before the spec ships in production CPUs.
Rangarajan explains this is driven by what AMD's GPUs need to run optimally.

AMD hasn't disclosed the ratio of CPUs to GPUs it's aiming for with Verano, so it's difficult to say how it compares to Nvidia. In a 2:1 ratio of GPUs to CPUs like we saw in Vera Rubin, Verano would deliver identical chip-to-chip bandwidth, while in a 1:4 ratio like we see in AMD's Helios racks, we'd be looking at about half the bandwidth at 448 GB/s. It's also not clear whether AMD has increased the number of xGMI links per I/O die for Verano or not, so bandwidth per GPU could be even higher. We expect more info closer to the MI500X's debut next year.
Part of a broader ecosystem

AMD doesn't expect Verano to replace Venice in every AI rack: The chip is designed specifically for use with Instinct accelerators. Moreover, AMD isn't waiting for Verano to roll out its Helios rackscale systems. As we discussed during Advancing AI earlier this year, those systems will feature 18 96-core Venice CPUs paired to 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs.

Moving forward, AMD expects its Venice to remain a popular host processor for AI head nodes not just for its own GPUs but for the growing number of homegrown accelerators built by the great model houses. ®

f4c9e9578fa302f7: MELAKA: DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke has challenged Barisan Nasional members of Parliament to resign from the cabinet instead of continuing to criticise the prime minister and the unity government while remaining in power.

In his first public appearance after stepping down as transport minister, Loke said those who disagreed with Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim's leadership should uphold the principle of collective responsibility by relinquishing their cabinet positions.
"If you are not happy, then leave. If you disagree with the prime minister, resign. I have done so. What about you, my friend?" Loke said during a ceramah here last night.
"Every day, you voice your disagreement, while your party attacks the Prime Minister day and night, claiming that one thing or another is wrong. Yet, you remain in the government.
"Every Wednesday and Friday, you attend cabinet meetings chaired by Anwar Ibrahim. What is this all about?" he added.
Loke also questioned why those dissatisfied with the government's policies and allocation decisions continued to remain in the administration instead of leaving.

"There are parties that are dissatisfied and criticise the government every day, questioning why certain ministries are not receiving allocations and raising other issues. Why are they still in the government? Why have they not left?" he said.

The Seremban member of Parliament also urged voters in Melaka to use their ballots in the state election to send a strong message to those pressuring Anwar to dissolve Parliament and pave the way for a general election.
"Although certain quarters are putting pressure on the prime minister to dissolve Parliament, we want to remind them that the mandate remains in Anwar's hands.
"If you are unhappy, you can leave.
"Even though I have resigned as a minister, I have pledged that all DAP MPs will continue to support Anwar. He will remain as Prime Minister," he said.
Although Loke did not mention anyone by name, his remarks appeared to be directed at BN chairman Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi.
It was previously reported that Zahid had said it would be better to dissolve Parliament and return the mandate to the people rather than reshuffle the cabinet.
The BN chairman, however, said he saw no need for a cabinet reshuffle at the moment.

Loke had earlier stepped down as transport minister with immediate effect following the Kuala Lumpur High Court's decision allowing former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak to serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest.
He said his resignation was in line with the principled stance he had previously announced.
01acc383015fdcbb: AS delegates attend the 31st cycle of the United Nations' climate pageantry, officially known as the Conference of Parties (COP), in Antalya, a familiar fatigue hangs over governments worldwide.
Critics question the effectiveness of the COP talks, while detractors ask if it is even necessary at this point.
While their sentiment is understandable, a more pragmatic position acknowledges the inherent limitations of the process while moving the needle forward – however slightly or slowly.
Nonetheless, because of multilayered interests, climate multilateralism has lost its focus as the talks have been co-opted by non-climate interests.
The "co-opting" by broader geopolitical and economic interests can be seen across the three different negotiation areas.
The examples showcase the obvious Global North and Global South divide, and the not so obvious struggle of who gets to dictate the industrial reboot of the 21st century.
First, the corporate hijacking of the just transition agenda threatens climate multilateralism by protecting high-emitting fossil fuel producers from phase-out mandates.
More than 5,300 fossil fuel lobbyists from 859 organisations attended COPs between 2021 and 2024, outnumbering most countries' delegations.
As a coalition of petro-state lawyers and corporate strategists have surmised, industry survival can be extended with semantics.
In this case, they have successfully shifted the focus of the just transition away from production phase-outs to emission mitigation.

This success bought the industry time and loopholes, validating risky energy sources like hydrogen and dubious emission-reduction technologies that allow the fossil fuel industry to delay net zero to another day.
Ultimately, the climate goals are preserved on paper, while the fossil fuels continue to be extracted from the ground.

Second, the replacement of public climate finance with private finance endangers climate multilateralism by allowing developed countries to outsource their legal responsibilities to the private sector.
The cost of climate change on the Global South runs in the trillions of dollars a year, while the current climate finance target is discounted at US$300 billion a year.

To address the financial discrepancy, Global North countries often note the insufficiencies of their public finance before delegating to private finance that are conveniently headquartered in their countries.

These private actors operate by their own commercial rules, utilising conventional credit frameworks that view Global South countries as high-risk investments and assigning them lower credit ratings that justify high borrowing costs.
Neither Global North countries nor private financiers are willing to admit the structural limits of private finance in climate action.
Operating on a piecemeal basis, private finance inherently lacks the coordination and mandate required for multi-decade structural transformation.
In short, instead of treating climate finance to right a historical wrong, proponents of private finance ensure that those who had the least to do with creating the crisis pay the price.
Third, allowing trade protectionism to inform climate negotiations risk fracturing multilateralism by prioritising industrial competitiveness over planetary survival.

Following an unprecedented mandate from the 2025 COP, the climate regime under the UN's Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) began exploring the intersection with global trade, which is an arena typically governed by the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
While seemingly aimed at addressing the climate change impacts on global trade, this new intersectional front could risk introducing competing institutional motivations.
Dialogues are held before official negotiations even begin to align divergent regimes – which exposed a fault line.
With the Global North favouring the WTO's technical and rules-based forums and the Global South insisting on adhering to UNFCCC's equity principles, this split gives ground for forum shopping.
Global North countries could bypass climate justice frameworks, opting instead for rules that prioritise trade.
If trade logic supersedes climate diplomacy in these formative talks, subsequent negotiations risk becoming a proxy battleground for trade protectionism under the guise of green stewardship.
To prevent this, the dialogue must anchor itself in UNFCCC principles.

Though the messiness looks typical of diplomatic friction, global climate multilateralism has turned into a high-stakes platform where Global North countries and their allies are increasingly shaping the substance and manner of these negotiations.
The irony, however, is that these powerful forces cannot control the messaging and narrative outside of the negotiation rooms because they cannot compel an increasingly sceptical and worried public.

For Malaysia at COP31 in Antalya, the path forward is to anchor negotiation strategies in domestic realities – such as capacity and financial gaps – and leverage the second Global Stocktake (GST-2) to systematically evaluate and expose policy loopholes utilised by Global North delegations.
As a comprehensive climate action progress report, GST-2 will dictate the trajectory of climate action over the next five years.
Until climate multilateralism is course-corrected, a hall in Antalya at COP31 will draft another elaborate mandate to chronicle what could have been and what should have been done.
* The writer is senior researcher at Institute of Strategic & International Studies (ISIS) Malaysia

f20f8d958aba1345: Evaluating the annual global temperatures each year requires context. There is a fair amount of natural variability from one year to the next, so it’s important to focus on the trend over time. Famously, global warming did not end in 1998, as some claimed a couple of decades ago—we just had a run of La-Niña-dominated years after a very strong El Niño.

Annual greenhouse gas emissions are much less variable, having increased fairly steadily, but many complicating factors can still muddy the picture. Sometimes those factors conspire to throw a year off the trend. It looks like 2026 will be one of those years.

A new analysis led by Corinne Le Quéré at the University of East Anglia estimates that fossil fuel emissions have fallen about 0.4 percent from last year. This probably isn’t a peak that symbolizes heartening progress on climate change, though; the researchers think it’s a short-term dip driven by the war in Iran and its effect on oil prices.

e0b89f1bdc725cde: President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency.
The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025.

LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024, having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017.

If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers.
It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit.

CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to reports. It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February.

With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. A strategy published last month emphasizes infrastructure whose failure would do the most damage, raising questions about what gets less attention as the agency operates with fewer staff.

LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting.

The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate.

Palantir, co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has become a major supplier of technology to US government agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Its work with immigration authorities has attracted criticism from civil liberties groups and Democratic lawmakers concerned about surveillance and the handling of sensitive personal information.

The controversy isn't confined to the US either. In the UK, WhatsApp messages obtained by campaign group Foxglove this week indicate that Palantir privately lobbied a health minister to consider extending its software into GP patient records, despite that data being expressly excluded from its £330 million NHS England contract for the Federated Data Platform.
That revelation follows news that NHS England wants greater oversight of Palantir's claims about the benefits of its software, amid questions over the evidence supporting its performance figures.
Those controversies could make LoSapio's confirmation hearings particularly interesting, especially as Democrats prepare to scrutinize Palantir's government business more closely.

It's unclear whether LoSapio plans to leave Palantir or what would happen to any financial interests he holds in the company if confirmed. Those are questions likely to come up during a confirmation process that CISA, having spent nearly two years without a permanent boss while losing a third of its workforce, could probably do without dragging on any longer. ®

7833de327fbac65a: LONDON: More women have come forward since the start of Russell Brand's rape and assault trial, a UK police chief said Tuesday, as the disgraced TV star began a 10-year jail sentence.
The reports of fresh complaints came as Brand's defence lawyer faced a storm of criticism for his comments and line of questioning in court, reopening the debate about victim shaming in Britain.

Detective Inspector Andy Furphy from the London Metropolitan Police said two further allegations against Brand were already being investigated and "we've had several reports in during the trial and since the verdict" on Thursday.

Brand, who has reinvented himself as an online Christian guru, was on Monday jailed for 10 years and six months after being found guilty of one rape and three sexual assaults committed against four women between 2004 and 2009.
The judge described him as a "sexual predator" who had shown "staggering arrogance" and "contempt" for his victims.

But defence lawyer Ian Winter has been sharply criticised for telling the trial Brand's victims were "not particularly vulnerable at all" and that he could not be guilty of rape as his accusers had not "resisted or screamed or even tried to leave."
UK deputy prime minister Lucy Powell said she found some of the defence's comments at the trial "incredibly depressing."
Support organisations said such tactics harked back to a previous era when victims were reluctant to come forward for fear of being quizzed in court on their behaviour and sexual history.
Victim Support said it had been "appalled, but not surprised, by the rape myths, misconceptions and stereotypes deployed by the defence" during Brand's trial.
It added that women should not have had to endure "disgraceful attempts to blame and discredit them" in court.

"Rape myths and stereotypes are still used day in, day out in sexual violence trials. The defendant's profile in this case has shone a spotlight on a systemic failing faced by victim-survivors across the country," it said.

Brand was charged last year after being exposed in 2023 by journalists from the Sunday Times, The Times and the Channel 4 Dispatches programme, leading to women coming forward to make complaints to police.
"Throughout Russell Brand's trial, we saw rape myths in action: Why didn't she scream? Why didn't she fight back?
"Why did she wait so long to report it? Why did she maintain contact with him afterwards?" wrote Ciara Bergman, head of Rape Crisis England & Wales, in The iPaper after Brand's conviction.
"These were all introduced as ways of discrediting the survivors and/or introducing doubt into the minds of jurors," she said.
Bergman, however, added the guilty verdict on the rape charge was "important" as the complainant had earlier had consensual sex with Brand.
"It suggests understanding among jurors that there is no such thing as blanket or automatic consent," she said.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Saturday the government must look at changing rape trials to "make sure they do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court as has been the experience of people in the past."
Describing Brand's actions as "horrifying", he pledged to introduce specialist rape and serious sexual offence teams in every police force by the end of 2027.
Rights of Women said the Brand trial highlighted the "urgent need for a trauma-informed justice system."
Giving evidence in court often meant women who had already "experienced significant trauma" were "re-victimised by the processes that should bring them both safety and justice", it said.

df2942aaef6d5f1f: ANTALYA: UN chief Antonio Guterres on Tuesday urged nations at COP31 to plan for a future without fossil fuels, even as summit hosts Turkey celebrated the discovery of new oil reserves.
Fossil fuels took centre stage at the UN climate summit where Turkey is seeking pledges to electrify the global economy rather than concrete new commitments to tackle coal, oil and gas.

Turkey's "electrification" push comes as scientists warned that emissions from burning fossil fuels – the primary driver of climate change – were projected to remain near-record highs for another year.
Guterres said "an accelerated transition away from fossil fuels is fundamental" to rein in global temperature rises on track to blow past the 1.5°C target in a matter of years.
"Let's be clear: fossil fuels are not only driving the climate crisis. Dependence on them carries a steep economic and security price, as the crisis in the Middle East has laid bare," he said.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan struck a different note on Monday, hailing the discovery of two oil fields – potentially containing 135 million barrels of crude – as "good news".
The contrast underscored a central challenge facing countries deadlocked over how quickly the world should move away from polluting fuels to cleaner forms of energy.
Since agreeing in 2023 for the first time to transition away from fossil fuels, nations have struggled to advance that goal at the annual COP conferences.
At last year's COP30 in Brazil, fossil fuels were not explicitly mentioned by name in the final agreement.
No major fossil fuel breakthrough is expected either from this year's negotiations between nearly 200 nations, which are being hosted by Turkey but chaired by Australia, itself a major coal exporter.
"Expectations are low – that's just a reflection of reality," the European Union's climate envoy Wopke Hoekstra said.

The leaders of a number of major economies are skipping the event, though Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg made her first COP appearance in several years to slam what she called "greenwashed circuses".
Difficult transition
After the lacklustre outcome last year, Brazil produced a much-anticipated report encouraging each country to choose its own path away from fossil fuels at their own pace.
"My last message is start now... don't wait. Planning is a good thing," said COP30 chief executive Ana Toni at an event promoting the voluntary "roadmap", which is not part of the COP31 negotiations.

Guterres urged countries to draw up plans with clear timelines for exiting fossil fuels: "Now, here at COP31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it, and delivering it," he said.
But many countries – particularly developing economies dependent on oil and gas revenue – have resisted these calls and stressed that each country should go at its own pace.
"We also have the right to develop. We cannot allow those assets to be stranded," said Antwi-Boasiako Amoah of Ghana, who chairs a group of African nations including oil-rich states.

Adao Soares Barbosa, who chairs the Least Developed Countries bloc, said it would be "very difficult" for the world's poorest nations to transition to clean energy without significant financial support.

Rather than revisiting this fraught debate, Turkey has sought to unite countries around a global goal to raise the share of final energy demand by electricity from around 20 percent to 35 percent by 2035.
On Tuesday, the hosts unveiled the first draft of this electrification pledge that stresses the use of "clean electricity and technologies" will differ among countries.
Officials from Germany, Ethiopia, Norway and Pakistan voiced support for the Turkish initiative.
Around one-third of electricity is produced using coal, and some nations have raised concerns that meeting this increased share with fossil fuels would not achieve climate aims.
"Of course, the cleaner that electrification is, the better it is," said Hoekstra.

d932cabd29603b4c: CAIRO: Egypt has had a military presence in Saudi Arabia for months, Cairo's top diplomat has said, two weeks after its parliament authorised helping defend the kingdom from Houthi attacks.

56edf5345860700d: SOFIA: Twelve people died and dozens were injured on Tuesday in a mass pileup in thick fog on a motorway in southeastern Bulgaria, whose roads rank as the most dangerous in the EU.

"We are actively working on equipping the toll system gantries with display screens to warn drivers," he said.

In total, 51 people were admitted to hospitals in nearby cities, with 13 of them critically injured, it added.

Bulgaria saw 71 road fatalities per million inhabitants in 2025, the highest rate in the European Union, according to European Commission figures.

In 2019, the EU introduced a target to reduce road deaths and serious injuries by 50 per cent by 2030.

44391e8f62a5409a: Fireworks AI has disclosed another cyberattack in October and a wider customer data exposure involving billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights.

Fireworks grouped the affected data into three categories:
Resource metadata: Resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation times, and more
Billing information: Billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment histories, account balances, and credit usages. Payment card numbers are not saved and therefore unaffected
Model weights and datasets: For certain customers, a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed, Fireworks said
Lin Qiao, Fireworks co-founder and CEO, said the apparent motive was not stealing model weights in response to concerns raised by Cantina Security CEO Hari Mulackal.
"From what we see attackers are not after weights," said Qiao. "Most downloads were partial and stopped."
Render founder and CEO Anurag Goel shared a notification from Notion warning that some chats with its AI assistant may have been exposed through the Fireworks incident.

"Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that your workspace, Render, was among the <1 percent of Notion workspaces that may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident," the email sent to Goel stated.
"Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed in this incident."

Notion said the exposed transcripts lacked separate information linking them to particular users or workspaces. As Reddit users pointed out, however, the conversations themselves could contain identifying details.

"Beyond what's in the chat transcript itself, there's no information tying the chat back to your workspace, users, or company," the email added. "No other data from within your workspace is affected."
Bloomberg reports that Fireworks is also working with customers including Cursor and Harvey to assess the impact.

Fireworks' update confirmed that it worked with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 team to remediate the attack, which included rotating credentials, isolating affected systems from the network, and tightening up data storage access and monitoring systems.
The update did not state how many customers were affected by either of the two attacks in October.

Fireworks first disclosed an incident on October 9 after detecting unauthorized use of internal credentials on October 6. Attackers accessed environment variables in evaluation jobs, including API keys and tokens belonging to some customers.

At the time, Fireworks said it had found no evidence of access to models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information. Monday's update substantially broadens the disclosed impact. ®

db18bae4f27ff05d: PETE Hegseth, a former National Guard officer who went from Fox News co-host to leading the world's most powerful military, is fighting to keep his job less than two years into his tenure as Pentagon chief.

The 46-year-old has survived a series of controversies as defence secretary, but many resurfaced in the articles of impeachment introduced on Monday by Thomas Massie, a Republican opponent of President Donald Trump who wants to remove Hegseth from office.
Hegseth said he was ready to defend his record.

"I couldn't be more proud of what our president has done, the decisions that he's made, the courageous calls that he's made, the bold nature of our... military leadership, the skill and courage of the troops on the ground," he said.
Hegseth, 46, has sought to transform the War Department — as Trump has unofficially renamed the Defence Department.

Deploying a combative and aggressive style, he has relentlessly targeted diversity, equity and inclusion efforts at the Pentagon and has fought to kick transgender troops out of the military and to bar others from joining.
"We are no longer the 'woke' department, or the weak department," said Hegseth in characteristically colourful remarks to troops earlier this year.
"No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals.
"Just warriors — just tough, ready, committed troops."

Several of the articles of impeachment relate to the Iran war, accusing Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution, which requires congressional consultation on and oversight of United States military interventions.
Hegseth is a vehement defender of the grinding, open-ended and widely unpopular conflict, which he has described as a "courageous and historic effort".

The Iran conflict was the fifth major international US military intervention under Hegseth, but unlike the first four, the war against Teheran has been neither quick nor bloodless from the American side, and has also wreaked economic havoc around the globe.

Heavily-tattooed Hegseth is a former infantry officer who spent more than 18 years in the National Guard and served in combat, deploying to Iraq and Afghanistan, and he often posts social media clips of himself working out with troops.
But he had no experience heading a large organisation before leading the Pentagon.

He came under fire during his confirmation process over alleged financial mismanagement at veterans' non-profits where he previously worked, as well as reports of excessive drinking and allegations of sexually assaulting a woman in California.

A few months after he took office, the Atlantic magazine revealed that its editor-in-chief was inadvertently included in a Signal chat in which Hegseth and other officials discussed imminent strikes on Yemen, with the Pentagon chief sending messages on the timing of the operation hours before it began.

Strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific have also been a source of controversy, especially an attack last year that left survivors who were killed in a follow-up strike.
Massie branded those attacks "extrajudicial killings" and said Hegseth "chilled independent legal review within the Defence Department".
In another contentious move under Hegseth, a number of senior military personnel, including the top-ranking general Charles "CQ" Brown, have been fired, often with little or no public explanation.
Hegseth has insisted that Trump is simply choosing the leaders he wants, but Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about politicisation of the traditionally neutral US military.

The defence chief, in a December 2025 speech, said the Pentagon "will not be distracted by democracy-building interventionism, undefined wars, regime change, climate change, woke moralising and feckless nation building".
"We will deter war. We will advance our interests. We will defend our people. Peace is our goal," he told the Reagan National Defence Forum.
But in January, US forces seized Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife in a shock raid in the capital Caracas.
Less than two months later, the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, a conflict that has since spread to countries around the Middle East.
Critics say the Iran war is the kind of military campaign Hegseth repeatedly denounced, but is now pursuing.

8da7fc5f08042e72: MALAYSIAN scholarship in the 1960s was fertile ground for academic titans like Tan Chee Khoon, Royal Professor Datuk Ungku Abdul Aziz and Professor Datuk Syed Hussein Al-Attas.

They were key to Malaysian universities becoming centres of intellectual rigour and critical debate while maintaining institutional autonomy. These figures bestrode Malaysian academia like rock stars, and the stature they attained during the post-Merdeka social revolution, notably at Universiti Malaya, has never been replicated.

In their heyday, UM's University Council, chaired by Tan, a legendary former member of parliament known popularly as "Mr Opposition", reflected left-leaning radicalism with an anti-colonial bent. Under Tan, the council leadership was shaped by merit and democratic representation, rather than political loyalty.
Instead of hiding away in ivory towers, they engaged in nation-building and criticised government policies while spearheading public discourse and powering socioeconomic reforms.
This intellectual bravado and hotbed of activism declined after the May 13, 1969 racial riots, particularly after the enactment of the Universities and University Colleges Act (Auku )in 1971.

Varsity budgets became strained, forcing decades of over-reliance on commercial partnerships or student-driven revenue. This led to a lack of specialised equipment, advanced research software and comprehensive digital resources.

Brain drain and a culture of mediocrity then resulted in our universities suffering in global rankings. After decades of pushback, the dons are now calling for academic freedom and better welfare in the proposed repeal of Auku.

There is opportunity now for universities to phase out unfair promotions and favouritism, and practices that undermine morale and meritocracy. Performance appraisals must recognise teaching, research, post-graduate supervision and societal contributions.

The proposed One Higher Education Act aims for fairer treatment, stronger grievance mechanisms and better accountability. Political appointments should be replaced with independent, peer-reviewed and merit-based ones. Faculty leaders must regain autonomy to manage curricula, departmental policies and student engagement.

Red tape must be slashed to focus on impactful research and mentorship. Funding should be directed towards competitive, programme-based grants, building better digital infrastructure, securing access to international scholarly databases and modernising laboratory facilities.

Eventually, the reforms should create public discourse without career-ending consequences. These reforms must also plug the brain drain by improving compensation, restoring critical thought and paving a transparent path for career advancement.
Ultimately, the overhaul must aim to recreate the halcyon years of the Tans, Ungku Azizes and Syed Husseins.
be627400228a56e0: GEORGE TOWN: Chet Singh, who helped turn Penang into a major electronics manufacturing hub, died today. He was 90.
His death was announced through a funeral notice posted on Gurdwara Sahib Bayan Baru's Facebook page.
Chet was the first general manager of Penang Development Corporation (PDC), serving from 1971 to 1991.
He worked closely with then chief minister Lim Chong Eu to bring foreign investors to Penang, which was struggling with unemployment following the loss of its free port status.

Their efforts helped attract companies such as Intel, AMD, Hewlett-Packard and National Semiconductor to Penang, laying the foundation for the electronics industry, which remains a major contributor to the country's economy.
Chong Eu credited Chet with the state's industrial success. “He is the father of Penang's industrialisation, not me,” he was quoted as saying in an account published by The Edge in 2010.
Chet was also associated with Gerakan, the party that governed Penang for nearly four decades, and served as a senator representing the state from 1996 to 1999.
Former chief minister Koh Tsu Koon recalled how Chet helped him attract investors after he took office in 1990.
Koh said Chet accompanied him on his first investment mission to Silicon Valley in the US, introducing him to major investors and advising him on persuading them to expand their operations in Penang.
Despite his stern appearance, Chet had a heart of gold and was always willing to help the poor and disadvantaged, Koh said.
Chet later worked with Lim Guan Eng's DAP-led administration, serving as a special adviser to the state government.

He oversaw the development of industrial estates and new townships, including Bayan Baru, and helped establish the Penang Skills Development Centre to train workers for the growing manufacturing sector.
Guan Eng described Chet as “one of Penang's finest sons”. “He had left an indelible mark on Penang's industrial footprint,” he told FMT.

He recalled how Chet persuaded him to approve the construction of a Sikh temple in Bayan Baru and said he hoped Chet's family would find comfort in remembering his contributions to Penang and its people.
A wake will be held at Chet's family home in Minden Heights from 9.30am tomorrow, followed by his last rites at the Batu Gantung Crematorium at 3pm.
d645eb1bcf64b3e9: NVIDIA chief executive officer Jensen Huang sits at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom, and the spy scandal that erupted over the weekend threatens to shake the company at a time when confidence in the AI investment frenzy is already fragile.

Taiwan-born Huang is regarded as the godfather of the AI economy, the executive every player in the industry must turn to because the technology depends on the graphics processing units (GPUs) that his company designs.
Those chips have made Nvidia one of the two most valuable companies in the world, alongside Apple.

GPUs are in short supply, and the most powerful tech executives and companies rely on Huang to keep them flowing to the data centres that run the models behind OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude.
Huang has also plowed Nvidia's windfall into AI startups and labs that spend the money on his chips, a circular arrangement that could spread any trouble at Nvidia across the industry.
"Nvidia without Jensen — I don't know what that's worth," Stephen Witt, author of a book on Huang and Nvidia, told CNBC. "Nvidia is Jensen Huang."

The scandal over Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy lands days before Anthropic's expected initial public offering, a Wall Street offering seen as a key test for an industry under pressure as investors show more caution in the AI story.
That wariness was fuelled by last week's United States elections, in which voters showed anger at AI, tech billionaires and the data centres that house Nvidia's chips.
Silicon Valley figures rallied to Huang's defence.

Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, wrote on X that Huang "did something incredibly dumb" that "was bad for America", but said he believed there had been no bad intention and that Huang was "irreplaceable for America's AI leadership".
"I simply do not believe he would ever knowingly do anything to disadvantage either America or Nvidia," said investor Gavin Baker, who has known Huang for almost 30 years.
Other investors were less confident Huang would survive the probe launched by the Nvidia board.

"I doubt Jensen Huang will be able to remain as Nvidia CEO," wrote Gary Black of the Future Fund, which counts Nvidia among its largest holdings, adding that Huang had "no natural successor within the company".
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co called it "a black eye moment" for Huang and said the Nvidia chief was "the core DNA of Nvidia".
"Jensen is not replaceable," said Ives, adding that he expected Huang to remain CEO in the near term but that the board's findings could still lead to his removal.
Huang's fate will likely be determined in Washington.
Ives said the scandal would spark multiple congressional inquiries and increase scrutiny of chip sales to China, a sensitive issue as the AI race between the US and China accelerates.
Huang had persuaded the Trump administration to ease restrictions on chip sales to China and, after donating to some White House causes, became a close adviser to President Donald Trump.

But Democrats won control of Congress in last week's elections, and China hawks from both parties are expected to ask why Trump did not act when he was first told of Huang's ties to the Chinese business-woman now suspected of spying for Beijing.
Bill Bishop, author of the Sinocism newsletter on China, said Huang's role in deciding who gets Nvidia's scarce chips made him a valuable target.
"With the new Congress, expect subpoenas and public hearings in which he is trashed and he and Nvidia are further damaged," Bishop wrote.
The scandal was "a win" for China's State Security Ministry, and Huang will now pay the consequences, he concluded.

698d649a93eed46b: JERUSALEM: Israel's new parliament convened Tuesday with plans to take aim immediately at caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as his rival Gadi Eisenkot vowed to quickly cobble together a new government.

Eisenkot, leading a broad left-to-right bloc, will control the agenda from the outset in the new parliament with the help of Israeli-Arab parties, although neither he nor the right-wing Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, holds a majority on their own.

"I am committed in this complex situation to form a national-emergency government as quickly as possible," Eisenkot, a 66-year-old former military chief who only recently entered politics, said before his swearing-in.
President Isaac Herzog, ceremonially opening the session, called on all sides to work together and avoid a fresh election in a deeply polarised country weary from three years of war.

Arab-Israeli lawmakers under fire
