8e2b588f812ac5a4: ATHENS: More than 100 foreign nationals have died since 2000 in Greek police stations or migrant centres with inadequate healthcare facilities, including 34 deaths that have not been officially registered, according to research published on Tuesday by Oxford University researchers.
In total, the research found 112 deaths in the 26-year period, including 44 suicides.
Of the 112 deaths, 84 occurred in police stations without medical staff and 27 were reported in migrant detention facilities.
The Greek government and the police ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The dataset, part of an ongoing project that monitors deaths of foreign nationals in detention, including those held on criminal grounds, draws on police statistics obtained through freedom of information requests, international monitoring reports, media and testimonies.
The findings reveal "gaps in official police records and serious barriers to healthcare, including in facilities receiving EU funding," the report's authors said in a statement.
They said 34 deaths documented by journalists, NGOs and monitors were not included in the police statistics.
The data, published on research platform Detention Landscapes, reflects complaints by human rights groups and follows a 2026 report by the Council of Europe's anti-torture committee (CPT).
The report said that deaths in police custody in Greece had increased and some could have been prevented with sufficient supervision, psychiatric care and healthcare.
Among the cases it examined was the death of a 37-year-old Pakistani migrant while in detention at an Athens police station.
The CPT also cited persistent overcrowding in prison cells, including five people in spaces meant for one, and detainees sleeping on concrete or bedbug-infested mattresses.

Greece, long a landing point for migrants trying to enter the European Union from Africa, Asia and the Middle East, told the CPT that it was taking steps to address deficiencies under a 2025-2030 action plan to improve detention conditions, protect prisoners' rights, boost staff and ease prison overcrowding, a problem in over 60 per cent of countries worldwide, according to a 2024 UN report.

0f696e8c856711df: Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. DeepMind's physical AI platform has several computational layers between user input and robotic action. There's the vision-language model piece, which is Gemini Embodied Reasoning. The other main component is the vision-language-action (VLA) that actually generates robot actions, like moving an actuator—that's Gemini Robotics, which has been bumped to version 2.5.

620ddfb5abecc278: The UK Post Office is extending its contract with Fujitsu to give it time to move services to a new supplier, after a scandal that has long marred the relationship between the two.
The current contract runs until March 2027, and the publicly owned company has announced a short, time-limited contract extension to cover the transition.

Accenture will take over running the Horizon system, which was at the center of a string of miscarriages of justice, from September 2027, after winning a £410 million contract in May this year. Meanwhile, the Post Office is developing a replacement for the aging system to serve its network of 11,500 branches.

The Post Office began rolling out the legacy Horizon IT system for accounting in 1999, along with two subsequent upgrades. The electronic point-of-sale (EPOS) and back-end finance system was first implemented by ICL, a UK tech firm majority-owned by Fujitsu in the 1990s and which it fully acquired in 1998. From 1999 until 2015, around 736 subpostmasters were wrongfully prosecuted and convicted over Horizon errors, devastating lives in the process.

The Post Office, Accenture, and Fujitsu have agreed that Fujitsu will hand over the operation of Horizon to Accenture between 1 June and 1 September 2027, with the final date set to be confirmed in March 2027.
Accenture is set to "walk in and take over" the current Horizon system by assuming day-to-day operations from Fujitsu, as well as developing the back-end of the new system to replace Horizon.

Post Office CEO Neil Brocklehurst said: "Ending our contract with Fujitsu is a critical milestone in Post Office's transformation, and today's agreement secures the transition away from Fujitsu and over to Accenture safely and responsibly to achieve our target of summer 2027.

"In addition to ending our contract with Fujitsu, we are also working at pace with our leading technology suppliers, Accenture, OneView Commerce, and Escher, to build a modern, resilient platform able to make everyday life easier for customers and postmasters for years to come."
Fujitsu has also been awarded a contract extension to run the UK Government's Emergency Alerts platform until October 2029. The contract is worth £9.6 million ($12.8 million).
The company committed to not bid for new public sector contracts while the inquiry into the Horizon scandal continues. ®
32a1d4cc4e65dfcd: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that popular obesity drugs—including Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound, and Mounjaro—may carry a "potential increased risk" of a rare eye condition that can lead to permanent vision loss.

In a drug safety communication Monday, the FDA said it will now require makers of GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs to add a warning about that risk on their drug labels. The specific eye condition it warns of is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or NAION. The condition is caused by restricted blood flow to the optic nerve, which leads to swelling and cell death and ultimately damages the nerve, causing abrupt vision loss that can often be permanent.

It's unknown how GLP-1 drugs may cause NAION. The condition is rare overall, occurring in somewhere between two and 10 people in 100,000 in the general population, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology. These small numbers have made it more difficult to determine with certainty if there is a connection. Further complicating the potential link is the fact that the risk factors for developing NAION are common among patients taking GLP-1 drugs. The risk factors include diabetes, cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, metabolic syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea.

68f66ac0cbd7169a: It was a fun few weeks while it lasted. People using both Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex to do AI-powered “reverse-engineering” or decompiling are now hitting guardrails or having their accounts limited while trying to do things like unbrick their internet-of-things devices or remove surveillance ads from their smart TVs.

Several people have reported triggering “safety checks” in Claude Code that prevented them from doing AI-powered reverse engineering; a highly upvoted Reddit post in r/ClaudeCode reads “The Dream is dead. Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is not likely to work with Claude.” A thread in the Reverse Engineer Anything Discord from last week reads, “Claude is refusing to decompile anything,” with multiple users responding saying they have hit similar walls. And X user log4j, who used OpenAI’s Codex to reverse engineer Samsung TVs, reported having their OpenAI account banned for violating its rules on “cyber abuse.” Other users said they asked Codex to reverse engineer hardware or their own code now say they have either been warned by the company or had their accounts restricted. A project called Decomp.wtf that made it easier to reverse engineer software and games has also shut down in recent days.

As we reported last month, Reverse Engineer-Anything has made it easy for people to use AI tools to hack electronics that they own and replace a manufacturer’s software or operating system with an open source or vibecoded one. People have installed new operating systems on their smart TVs, have turned baby monitors into AI assistants, have unbricked internet-of-things devices that were abandoned by their manufacturers, and have installed new software on very old hardware. At the time, I wasn’t sure how I felt about the trend, but as I’ve seen people take ownership and control back over the devices that manufacturers have purposefully bricked, turned into spyware, or have placed artificial limitations on, I have come to see AI-powered reverse engineering of electronic devices as one of the few LLM uses genuinely worth getting excited about. And so big companies have immediately taken steps to restrict this behavior.

The policy tweaks show that big AI corporations will protect other big corporations when their users find ways to use LLMs to circumvent the artificial constraints that hardware manufacturers put on their devices. AI-powered copyright circumvention is OK with big tech when it’s a massive company scraping the entire internet to build their LLMs, but is not OK when people then use those tools to liberate their internet-of-things devices. It’s not the end of AI-powered reverse engineering, but people suddenly getting locked out of their accounts for asking AI to reverse engineer their gadgets suggests that the future of this practice lies in open weight, local, and uncensored models, making it less accessible to the masses and the people who could probably benefit from it most.

Tarun Gogineni, an OpenAI engineer, tweeted that people are not supposed to have their OpenAI accounts restricted for reverse engineering: “these blocks are mostly accidental and a result of difficult decision boundaries; there is no prohibition against reverse engineering with codex. it’s getting fixed,” he tweeted.

But people who are doing AI-powered reverse-engineering suggest that they are moving away from big companies’ models to alternatives where they aren’t going to have their accounts disabled or have to figure out how to work around AI company guardrails.

“My general experience about reverse-engineering getting blocked has been more or less 100% correlated with the ‘cyber’ category blocks I have received. My take is that the lab[s] are probably under pressure to not have their models take part in some kind of criminal hacking activities and their cyber guardrails are erring on the side of being too strict,” Matt Brown, principal consultant at Brown Fine Security and someone who has been using AI to reverse-engineer devices, told 404 Media. “I am investing in hardware and trying to stay up to speed because the frontier labs guardrails will randomly change without warning on the same model. For my security research and pentesting work I really don’t want to invest tooling and energy into an ecosystem that will eventually lock me out. These guardrails on the frontier side have come at the same time as open weight models from (mostly) China are getting better and better.”

Brown posted a YouTube video last week explaining how he found hidden Bluetooth commands in an internet-of-things gas monitor attached to his propane tank with the open weight model GLM 5.3. He has explained in various posts that the guardrails big companies are putting on reverse engineering are why local AI and open weight models are important.

AI-powered reverse-engineering isn’t going anywhere, but it does look like it’s going to become much harder to use the most popular frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic for it. It’s unclear how much longer it will be possible for you to open an OpenAI Codex window, ask it to find a smart TV hooked up to your network, and tell it to install a new operating system on it. Moving forward, it looks like this type of work will be best done with open source, open weight, uncensored, and local models. That’s a bummer, because one of the things that was so exciting about the Reverse Engineer-Anything trend was how easily accessible it had become.

Last month, researchers and law professors at Cornell Tech, Columbia University, and New York University published a paper about how cheap, AI-assisted reverse-engineering is challenging big manufacturers’ dominance over the devices their make, and is challenging existing intellectual property law.

“AI systems can identify hardware components, extract firmware, decompile object code, and clone entire apps. The resulting struggle between technology vendors and reverse engineers will challenge a wide range of laws, including trade secret, copyright, anti-circumvention, computer misuse, and contract,” they write. “The law of reverse engineering was built for a world where opening a device took time, tools, and rare expertise. That friction is vanishing as agents whittle endless, precise picks for the many little locks that fill our digital lives.”

In recent days, people have started modifying older digital cameras with new, vibe-coded operating systems. In a video about hacking old cameras, the YouTuber Breno Loves Cameras explains why it’s such a big deal and why camera companies don’t like it; that same logic can be applied to any device manufacturer.

“Camera companies have this practice of keeping features to release on newer cameras, and having distinctions [in features] in camera lines,” the YouTuber Breno said in one video. “This is breaking that from those big companies, which are going to lose a lot of money if this becomes a big thing.”

Through that lens, it’s easy to see why big companies are protecting other big companies. People finally found a thing to do with AI tools that gives consumers a bit more control over the devices they bought; it must be immediately stamped out.

“This vibe-code hacking is only called ‘reverse’ when somebody who lacks a trillion dollars is doing it,” the science fiction author Bruce Sterling tweeted. “When you ‘reverse engineer’ the entire Internet Common Crawl, you just built a nice AI model.”

4ac67656f256b571: From Jamaluddin Aziz

The announcement that the Islamic development department (Jakim) and central committee for applications for filming and performances by foreign artistes (Puspal) are investigating alleged elements of ritualistic worship at The Weeknd’s recent concerts at the Bukit Jalil national stadium highlights a recurring cultural tension in Malaysia.
As a critical media scholar, I view this controversy not merely as a clash over entertainment guidelines, but as a textbook case of “context collapse”.

Coined by media researcher Danah Boyd and further theorised with Alice Marwick in their seminal 2011 study in New Media & Society (“I tweet honestly, I tweet passionately: Twitter users, context collapse, and the imagined audience”), context collapse occurs when digital platforms flatten multiple, distinct audiences into a single space.

When content created for one specific cultural or artistic environment is stripped of its original framing and judged within an entirely different moral or ideological context, modern pop theatrics are easily misread as literal religious devotion.

To understand how context shapes interpretation, one need only compare The Weeknd’s Nov 4 and 5 shows with another massive event held at the exact same stadium just three weeks earlier: Konsert Tradisional Gema Bumantara by Biduanita Negara Siti Nurhaliza.
Both concerts drew tens of thousands of devoted fans who sang every lyric in unison and cheered wildly for their favourite performer.
Yet, the public and institutional reactions to these two sold-out spectacles could not have been more different.

In modern pop culture, intense audience enthusiasm is often loosely referred to as “fan worship”. Historically, words like “fan” (from the Latin fanaticus, meaning temple frenzy) and “icon” (from the Greek eikōn, meaning sacred image) do share etymological roots in ancient religious practice.
Today, however, these terms describe secular cultural admiration. When fans cheer at a stadium, they are participating in collective musical enjoyment, not a spiritual ritual.

Viewing both Bukit Jalil concerts through a critical media lens reveals three key dynamics driving these divergent reactions. First is the mechanics of context collapse. Critics of The Weeknd’s concert pointed to short social media clips showing a towering golden female robot sculpture and dancers in red hooded robes as evidence of pagan or machine-worship rituals.

As Marwick and Boyd’s framework demonstrates, when these visuals are detached from the full two-hour concert narrative and circulated online to audiences unfamiliar with Western pop-art tropes, context collapses.
Stripped of their theatrical framing, a futuristic sculpture by Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama meant to critique the hollowness of fame and materialism is flattened into a literal religious idol.

Second is embedded cultural context. In contrast, Siti’s concert operated within a shared, deeply understood local framework. Utilising classical floral visuals and orchestral staging without human statues, her performance aligned seamlessly with Malaysian cultural and religious norms.

Because audiences and regulators immediately understood the context of Irama Malaysia heritage, the collective euphoria in the stadium was celebrated as patriotic pride rather than scrutinised as spiritual misdirection.

At most, conservative critiques of such local shows rarely go beyond general moral cautions against lagha (worldly distraction or frivolous amusement), a far cry from the theological panic of syirik (idolatry) projected onto The Weeknd’s unfamiliar pop symbolism.
Third is audience literacy and intent. Context collapse assumes that audiences are passive consumers who absorb imagery literally.
In reality, modern concertgoers possess high media literacy. Tens of thousands of Malaysians attended The Weeknd’s show to experience Grammy-winning music and dystopian sci-fi stagecraft.

Treating theatrical props as acts of syirik (idolatry) ignores the crucial distinction between artistic metaphor and religious intent (niat), unfairly questioning the faith and intelligence of ordinary Malaysian fans.
Puspal plays an essential role in ensuring that international performances respect Malaysia’s laws and social harmony.
However, effective regulation in the digital age requires media literacy and a resistance to reactionary interpretations born out of viral, out-of-context video clips.

If Malaysia wishes to remain a premier destination for global live entertainment, bringing vital economic and tourism benefits to Kuala Lumpur, authorities must evaluate performances within their full artistic context.
Distinguishing between pop-culture symbolism and actual religious worship is not just good cultural policy; it is essential for fair and rational governance.
Jamaluddin Aziz is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

125f71cc5c438b02: TUARAN, Nov 10 — After more than a decade carrying a firearm to safeguard national security, Hayword Losuil has taken a different path, turning his attention to safeguarding the country's food security as an agricultural entrepreneur, supplying bird’s eye chillies to the community.

Admitting that it was not easy to take off the Malaysian Army uniform he had worn since 2008, the 38-year-old Sabahan said his deep passion for agriculture eventually strengthened his resolve to venture into a field closer to his heart.

“I ended my service in the Malaysian Armed Forces in 2022. Armed with the knowledge gained from a farming course organised by the Armed Forces Fund Board (Perhebat) in Sungai Buloh, Selangor, I gradually developed KDO Farm in 2023,” he told Bernama at his farm in Kampung Tompinahaton, Kiulu, here.

Located about 47 kilometres northeast of Kota Kinabalu, Kiulu, a sub-district of Tuaran, is not only renowned for its picturesque green valleys, community-based rural tourism and white-water rafting activities, but also holds tremendous potential as an agricultural hub in Sabah.

Recognising its geographical advantages and the consistently strong market demand for bird’s eye chillies in Tuaran, Tamparuli and Kiulu, Hayword was determined to fully harness the fertility of Kiulu’s land.

“My interest in this venture developed after I saw the potential of the crop, which enjoys stable market demand. This motivated me to produce quality chillies using good agricultural practices,” said the Kiulu-born entrepreneur.
Military discipline
His daily routine begins while the morning mist still blankets the picturesque Kiulu valley.
Hayword starts work by inspecting the fertigation system, checking the fertiliser mixture and looking for signs of diseases and pest infestations among the rows of bird’s eye chilli plants.
The discipline instilled during his 14 years in the military is now fully applied to managing his farm.

“Experience in the uniformed services has shaped my discipline considerably. Work must follow a schedule, be punctual, clean and consistent. Crops cannot wait for us; we have to take care of them at all times,” he said.
The same discipline is reflected in his financial management.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Farmer and entrepreneur Hayword Losuil shows bird’s eye chillies harvested from his farm in Kampung Tompinahaton, Kiulu, on November 10, 2026.
Starting small with RM5,000 of his own capital, Hayword did not expect to generate substantial returns overnight.
Instead, he reinvested his modest profits to gradually expand the farm.

“I started with just 100 polybags before increasing the number to 256 within two years of setting up the farm in 2023,” said Hayword, who now cultivates about 1,000 bird’s eye chilli plants on his own 0.08-hectare plot.

His firmly held philosophy of “making small profits, reinvesting and expanding gradually” has paid off, with KDO Farm now owning business assets, including fertigation equipment purchased from its earnings, worth nearly RM35,000.
The science of cultivation
The cultivation of bird’s eye chillies at KDO Farm follows a carefully planned schedule to ensure the quality of the plants and the grade of the produce.

The seeds are first sown in special trays for 21 to 30 days before being transferred into polybags once the seedlings have passed the critical stage of initial root and leaf development, allowing for optimal growth.

According to Hayword, bird’s eye chilli plants typically begin producing fruit as early as 60 days after planting (DAP) and can continue bearing fruit for up to 300 DAP, depending on daily care and the plants’ resilience against environmental threats.
Adherence to Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) has enabled KDO Farm to record an average production of between 50 and 60 kilogrammes of fresh chillies per week during peak season.
“Production depends largely on the age of the plants, weather conditions and daily maintenance. Once the plants mature, yields become more consistent,” he said.
In terms of income, he said KDO Farm could earn between RM2,000 and RM3,000 per harvest, depending on prevailing market prices.

“When market prices rise, profits naturally increase. However, when prices fall, we have to manage input costs more efficiently and carefully to ensure the business remains competitive,” he said, adding that sales of bird’s eye chillies were among his family’s main sources of income.
Encouraged by the fruits of his labour, Hayword plans to diversify his crops by venturing into ginger cultivation in the near future.
Overcoming challenges

Farming comes with its own set of challenges, and Hayword has had his share of difficulties, including changing weather conditions, fungal diseases and pest attacks, all of which can affect production and crop quality.
Rising agricultural input costs, particularly fertilisers and pesticides, have also placed additional pressure on the farm’s financial management.

To prevent these risks from undermining his hard work, Hayword conducts regular farm inspections, uses balanced fertilisers, implements pest control measures in accordance with strict standard operating procedures and ensures that the farm environment remains clean.

At the same time, he continuously seeks new knowledge from various sources while strengthening KDO Farm through ongoing technical advice and guidance from officers of the Tuaran Area Farmers’ Organisation (PPK).
Through PPK Tuaran, Hayword has gained knowledge of GAP, modern farm management and marketing strategies suited to current market demands.
Digital marketing
To expand the market for his bird’s eye chillies, Hayword does not rely solely on direct sales to wholesalers and local buyers in Tuaran, Tamparuli and Kiulu.

Keeping pace with technological developments, he actively leverages social media platforms such as Facebook, WhatsApp and TikTok to promote his produce and build greater customer confidence in the KDO Farm brand.

In line with his long-term business plans, he has also taken another step forward by developing value-added products to reduce his dependence on fresh chilli sales, which are vulnerable to market price fluctuations.
Under the KDO Farm brand, Hayword is developing downstream products such as sambal tuhau and pure ground chilli paste.

“Sambal tuhau was chosen because it is a unique product closely associated with Sabah’s identity and culinary heritage. I want the chillies from my farm to be more than just fresh produce for sale; I want them processed into value-added products that promote local produce,” he said.
Hayword’s hard work has also benefited the local community, with residents being engaged to help harvest the chillies during peak seasons.
No need to rush

The success of the Kiulu native in developing his chilli farm demonstrates that limited land or a lack of prior agricultural experience need not be obstacles to becoming an agricultural entrepreneur, provided one has strong discipline, perseverance and a willingness to continuously acquire new knowledge.

At the end of the interview, Hayword shared some words of advice and encouragement for fellow former security personnel who are about to retire or have recently completed their service in the uniformed forces.

“My advice to fellow veterans is to start small, draw on the discipline you already have, keep learning and never give up easily. With consistent effort, agriculture can grow into a highly successful business,” he said. — Bernama
a7ed8c3ef7e0a90a: TOKYO, Nov 10 — A Tokyo court dismissed today Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa’s lawsuit against US tech giant Meta and its Japan unit over the use of his name and image in fraudulent investment ads on their platforms.

Online fraudsters commonly use Maezawa’s name and picture without his permission to lure victims. One typical advert captions his image: “Started with 10,000 yen (RM256). Gained 1.3 million yen in four days.”
Maezawa, the founder of Japan’s largest online clothing retailer, filed the lawsuit in 2024, saying Meta was “not making efforts” to stop the incidents.
He said at the time he sought to “clarify whether their actions are legal or not” and demanded just one yen in damages.

Meta argued that unidentified posters had placed the advertisements and said the company had no obligation to constantly monitor content in order to detect and remove rights-infringing material, according to public broadcaster NHK.
The Tokyo District Court today “turned down the plaintiff’s claims”, a court spokesman told AFP.
The ruling was made on the grounds that Meta “is merely a platform operator and was not directly involved in the posting of the ads”, private broadcaster TBS reported.
The court, however, acknowledged Maezawa’s publicity rights and portrait rights had been infringed, TBS said.
Neither Maezawa nor Meta could immediately be reached for comment on the ruling.
But Maezawa’s lawyer told reporters after the decision that “the number of scam ads has not decreased, and even now we are detecting a considerable number of scam ads featuring Mr. Maezawa”.

“With this ruling, I’m worried we’ll end up with a society where people think, ‘So in the end, even if you fight in court, it’s useless,’ and quietly resign themselves to their losses,” the lawyer said, according to TBS. — AFP
f1df53589a9957e8: ACCRA, Nov 10 — An acrid haze hung over a sprawling dump in Ghana’s capital, Accra, as excavators gouged into mounds of smouldering rubbish.
Thin plumes of black smoke curled from burning plastic and rubber, mingling with the rank odour of stagnant lagoon water.

At Agbogbloshie, a district on the Korle Lagoon delta, thousands of tonnes of refuse have accumulated over decades, overwhelming the fragile wetlands overlooking a slum of around 80,000 residents, many of them migrants and traders.
For scrap dealer James Hassan, a 31-year-old Liberian immigrant, it is both his home and livelihood.
Without gloves or a mask, he sifts daily through piles of unwanted electronics and metal for scraps to sell.
The skin on his palms is thickened and scarred from cuts and rashes but he has become accustomed to the pain and discomfort.
“I have headaches and coughs after long days under the sun, but I have never sought medical care. I feel they are normal,” he told AFP.
Environmental health experts say that workers are exposed to toxic metals and chemicals through skin cuts, inhaling waste smoke and dust.

While no study as yet links specific diseases to Agbogbloshie’s pollution, “the cumulative contamination raises concern even if precise causal chains remain unquantified,” epidemiologist Reginald Quansah, of the University of Ghana, said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Scrap dealers offload electronic waste at the Agbogbloshie scrapyard in Accra, on October 3, 2026. — AFP
Global pipeline of waste
Waste management is a prominent theme at the COP31 climate talks, which began in Turkey on Monday.
Agbogbloshie’s refuse comes largely from beyond Ghana’s borders.
Accra’s huge second-hand clothing market has imports from Europe, North America and Asia — but often with a troubling byproduct.
“A lot of clothes that are shipped into Ghana come as waste,” Greenpeace Africa’s head of investigations Samuel Quashie-Idun told AFP.
Greenpeace estimates that 15 million used garments arrive in Ghana each week.
Even after traders extract what they can sell, roughly half ends up as “dead waste” dumped on beaches and fields or burned, it said.
One study Greenpeace cited put Ghana’s used clothing imports at over 110,000 tonnes in 2022.
For the country’s 35 million people, “these volumes far exceed local demand and... burdens waste systems,” Quashie-Idun said.

Greenpeace found that 89 per cent of sampled “dead” garments contained petrochemical fibres such as polyester, which shed microplastics as they decay, and release carcinogens hundreds of times above safe levels in smoke when the textiles are burnt.
“This is not just an environmental crisis... it’s also a human health crisis,” said Hellen Kahaso Dena, Greenpeace’s plastics project expert.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A volunteer from Greenpeace collect textile waste on James Town beach in Accra, on October 2, 2026. — AFP
‘Fashion waste dumping ground’
“The global north is effectively using Ghana as a dumping ground for fashion waste,” she told AFP.
The metals and electronics tell a similar story.
Runoff from Accra pours into Korle Lagoon beside Agbogbloshie, making it one of the city’s most polluted waterways.
Here, old fridges, TVs and appliances are crudely recycled.
Scrap dealer Barima Okuanaju pulls apart refrigerators and cars by hand, recovering copper wiring, aluminium panels and iron parts to sell.
He makes about 50-100 cedi (RM16.2-RM36.5) a day.
While he mines every inch of wire and circuit boards, polluting fumes rise around him.
Burning computer cables and batteries release lead, mercury and other toxins; open fires emit soot and dioxins that communities breathe in.
At a market in Agbogbloshie, stalls ring the dump, where women and children sell food, tools and water, amid the smoke.
Fourteen-year-old Aminatu Fatawu sells bottled water to the dump workers.
The smoke makes her cough and lately she has noticed blood in her saliva.
“The boys here are always burning... it always makes me cough. When I spit, there’s blood sometimes,” she said.
Her mother allows her to work to help cover her school fees, she said.
Those working at Agbogbloshie face lung and neurological health conditions, Quansah, the epidemiologist, said.
Scientists warn that contamination from the dump seeps into the lagoon and soil, ending up in the food chain and potentially affecting local diets for years to come.
In September, President John Mahama launched a three-month cleanup to remove about one million tonnes of waste from Agbogbloshie.

Heavy military and public works equipment has begun hauling garbage to a landfill about 50 kilometres (31 miles) outside Accra, where it will be compacted and covered under strict environmental safeguards.
Informal workers won’t be forgotten, Local Government Minister Mahama Ayariga said.
He plans to bring garbage pickers and tricycle hauliers into the formal recycling process and hopes “to create up to 20,000 permanent jobs in waste management and the circular economy”.
Nevertheless, the scavengers feel uncertain about the future.

ee5e0cf57a29ffec: TOKYO, Nov 10 — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair, reportedly with a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based company that the US suspects of smuggling AI microchips into China.
The scandal has focused attention on how China, a major artificial-intelligence power in itself, obtains the cutting-edge chips despite US export restrictions.
Why are Nvidia chips so important?
Nvidia designs advanced components originally created to handle 3D visuals in video games, called Graphics Processing Units (GPUs).
These have the power to crunch colossal amounts of digital data, so are also used at scale to train and run artificial intelligence.
ChatGPT’s 2022 launch showcased the potential of AI, sparking an investment gold rush as governments and tech giants raced to develop the technology further.
With chip orders pouring in, Nvidia’s market valuation has soared to US$4.5 trillion (RM18.24 trillion) — currently on par with Apple as the world’s two most valuable companies.
Which chips does the US restrict?
Washington bans the export of Nvidia’s top-end “Blackwell” and “Rubin” GPUs to China, citing security concerns, as advanced AI has military applications.
The policy also allows the US’s top AI labs to maintain their global lead.
Huang has lobbied the US government to allow Nvidia chip sales to China, warning that the restrictions are fuelling the rise of competitive homegrown alternatives.
This year Washington eased controls on Nvidia’s previously banned — and less powerful — “H200” chip, with the US taking a 25 per cent cut of sales.
But US conditions have made it difficult for shipments to be approved, with Beijing also reportedly reluctant to buy H200s as its own chip industry gains momentum.
How does China get its chips?
Recent launches of high-performing models from Chinese startups, including Moonshot AI, Z.ai and DeepSeek, have turned up the heat on US rivals.
“Chinese vendors are still using cutting-edge Nvidia chips to train their models” despite the controls, Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at Omdia, told AFP.

Chips may be smuggled into the country, or accessed through a loophole that allows Chinese firms to rent out computing power at data centres stuffed with Nvidia chips in a third nation, often Southeast Asian.
“US export controls restrict where a chip is shipped, not who uses it,” explained Stephen Wu, founder of the Carthage Capital investment fund.
That means Nvidia GPUs can sit in Malaysia’s Johor region, for example, “in full compliance while a customer in Shenzhen logs in”, Wu told AFP.
White House adviser Michael Kratsios said this summer that Moonshot AI had accessed high-end Nvidia chips in Thailand.
Washington has also accused Chinese AI labs of training systems to mimic the capabilities of US models.
And then there is the big question of smuggling.
Tech outlet The Information said in December that DeepSeek developed its new model using thousands of chips dismantled overseas and brought into China.
DeepSeek did not respond to a comment request at the time. Nvidia told The Information they had not seen evidence of such smuggling which “seems far-fetched”.
How about Chinese chips?
“Nvidia chips still make top-level AI work faster and easier, but they are no longer the only path,” said Poe Zhao, founder of analysis publication Hello China Tech.
“The open question is cost” as “training on Chinese chips usually takes more time and more engineering”.
Huawei is China’s top Nvidia competitor, although it lags behind the US titan, and DeepSeek will reportedly train its next major AI model on Huawei chips.
“Chinese-made chips are improving fast”, Su said, with more collaborations likely to come.
Huawei said in September its next-generation AI chip would be ready in the first quarter of 2027, three quarters earlier than planned.
To boost the power of Chinese-made chips, AI companies need to use more of them, Wu said.
“They pay for it in power and cost — which they can afford, because Chinese electricity is cheap and the chips are state-subsidised.” — AFP
506e3fe2297dc404: Twelve years into Stanford's 100-year study of artificial intelligence, the project's third report raises more questions than it answers.
The 2026 AI100 Study Panel report acknowledges its limitations in its twelfth takeaway: "This report will be out of date by the time you read it."

But it's nonetheless a worthwhile exercise for those who haven't been paying close attention to the development of machine learning over the past few years and for policymakers who may benefit from a review of AI's metastatic growth.

"The last five years constitute a watershed moment in the history of AI," said Professor Sheila McIlraith, chair of the AI100 Standing Committee, in a statement. "This report examines what led to the extraordinary capabilities of today's AI systems, and how they are reshaping society. As we look ahead, we anticipate continued increase in AI capabilities alongside transformative advances in science and medicine.

"Rapid change will challenge governments and industry to support and safeguard our people, our institutions, and our critical infrastructure. Both the benefits and the risks of AI technologies require the same clear-eyed scrutiny."

Established in 2014, the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) is overseen by a Standing Committee of AI experts and administered by Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI). It's charged with producing reports every five years, the first of which debuted in 2016.
The 2026 report's other key points highlight the transformation brought about by increasingly capable machine learning software.
It identifies scaling as the engine of AI's advance, but also points to the growing cost and difficulty of obtaining training data as constraints on further progress.

The report likens AI's disruptive potential to that of the World Wide Web – without dwelling on the irony that the web itself is among the things being disrupted. It points to creative industries, computer programming, and mathematics as fields once deemed beyond the reach of automation that are now being upended.

Science, the report says, is being transformed by AI as it accelerates research timelines and opens up novel challenges. At the same time, the report cautions that "we will need to understand how AI-mediated information environments reshape collective cognition and moral behavior." The recent retraction of some 1,400 scholarly papers for failure to meet academic standards highlights the urgency of that message.

Then there's the AI investment boom and "fears of a financial bubble," which won't be assuaged by recent NASDAQ volatility and revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged intelligence operative for China.
Concerns about the concentration of frontier AI development, the pressure AI puts on cybersecurity, and the active use of AI for military applications are also noted in the report.
So too are worries about what AI-generated media does to trust.
Item nine on the report's takeaway list is perhaps the most noteworthy: "AI is reshaping the lives of billions of people, yet the public has had little say in how it is developed and deployed."
The recent US midterms suggest voters are finding ways to make themselves heard about AI datacenters, even if that falls short of shaping broader AI policy.

Item ten posits that longstanding academic concerns about AI bias, ethics, and safety are beginning to converge with what until recently seemed like worries inspired by speculative fiction, such as AI agents hacking into companies without human oversight.

And item 11 frames the entire report by calling out the lack of a coherent regulatory response to AI: "AI governance is fragmented and increasingly framed in terms of national security, with little international consensus among states on its direction."
Those takeaways introduce the AI100 Study Panel's examination of 12 standing questions about what AI makes possible and how humans are handling it. Easy answers are in short supply.
But as the report's disclosure section makes clear, even the people taking the century-long view are using the technology to assess itself.
"Reflecting the progress in AI over the period this report covers, AI tools were used extensively in its production," the report explains.

"The report was written by humans, and its authors used AI primarily to transcribe and summarize meetings, support dictation, and check drafts for typos, consistency, duplication, tone, and structure. In some cases, AI suggested rewording of human-written text. AI was also used to compare this report with previous AI100 reports, identifying where expectations and reality have diverged or converged over five years. After completion, AI tools checked for inadvertent plagiarism and signs of AI-generated content." ®
6d8a5fdc4a818f0c: PUTRAJAYA: The public has been advised to postpone all water recreational activities, including bathing, swimming, picnicking and camping, at rivers, rapids, waterfalls and irrigation canals throughout the 2026/2027 Northeast Monsoon season.

In a statement, the Malaysian Fire and Rescue Department said unpredictable weather conditions, coupled with heavy and prolonged rainfall in several areas, could cause sudden rises in water levels, strong currents and water surges, posing serious risks to public safety.
"Water surges can occur in the blink of an eye. Do not wait until the current becomes strong before taking action. Safety and the preservation of life must always be the priority," it said.
The department reminded the public to stay alert to weather developments, follow instructions from the authorities and take preventive measures to avoid untoward incidents.
"In the event of an emergency, the public should immediately call the 999 emergency hotline and provide the location of the incident to rescue personnel," it said.
The department also conveyed its condolences and sympathies to the families of victims involved in a water surge incident at Sungai Pertak, Kuala Kubu Bharu, Selangor, yesterday.
Eight people were reported to have been swept away by strong currents while engaging in recreational and hiking activities in the surrounding area.
Another 26 people who were stranded near the incident site were rescued by emergency response teams.

"This incident serves as another serious reminder that recreational activities in rivers and forest areas carry significant safety risks, particularly during unpredictable weather conditions throughout the monsoon season," JBPM said.

0834437ac5e857ba: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — Former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak has arrived at his residence in Jalan Langgak Duta here today to begin serving the remainder of his SRC International prison sentence under house arrest.
Najib’s arrival at his Taman Duta home followed a fresh High Court order this afternoon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence at the residence until August 23, 2028.

He arrived at his residence at about 9.25pm in a silver SUV, accompanied by a convoy of several vehicles believed to be carrying security personnel, which escorted him into the compound as reporters waited outside.

Earlier today, High Court judge Datuk Aslam Zainuddin directed the Court Registrar to issue a new warrant of release after hearing submissions from Najib’s lawyers and Deputy Public Prosecutors.
Aslam said the new order cancelled the November 5 order and replaced it with one allowing Najib to serve the remainder of his sentence at home.
A vehicle believed to be carrying former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak arrives at his residence in Jalan Langgak Duta, Kuala Lumpur on November 10, 2026. — Picture by Firdaus Latif
The fresh order came after the Attorney-General’s Chambers sought a review of the previous court order, saying clarification was needed over its wording and legal effect.
Najib had remained at Kajang Prison despite an earlier court order paving the way for his house arrest, after the AGC said implementation should be deferred pending legal clarification.

The former prime minister’s conditional royal pardon, granted on September 18, allows him to serve the remainder of his SRC International sentence under house arrest until August 23, 2028, subject to the stipulated conditions.
The arrangement followed the payment of the RM50 million fine imposed on Najib in the SRC International case.

Najib was initially sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment and fined RM210 million in 2020. The Federal Territories Pardons Board reduced his sentence to six years and the fine to RM50 million in January 2024.
08367870b5ce119e: A series of tax cuts since President George W. Bush's 2001 legislation have helped push the national debt to US$32 trillion. AP Photo/Ron EdmondsDemocrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U.S. economy. Clocking in at US$32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living. Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes. Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt. The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found. The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar, I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact. But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper, the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts. I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing. It’s all relative Proponents of fiscal austerity argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise. U.S. federal spending, however, has remained relatively flat – outside of emergencies like the 2009 recovery package and COVID-19 stimulus funds – even as GDP has risen. At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a study by the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan think tank, noted. President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2.9% of GDP, according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis. The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1.8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth. Coming in sixth place at 1.2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts. Costly extensions While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91.2% to 97.1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall 10-year cost of $1.5 trillion. That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025. But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through Trump’s legislation that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts. The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would add another $3.4 trillion over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to 116% of GDP by the end of 2034. Why deficits and economic growth matter so much A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not. If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, debt remains stable. The problem for the U.S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while interest payments on government debt are rising as well. This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U.S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with lower tax revenue due to tax cuts, the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office. In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U.S. took in more tax revenue than it spent and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats. It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U.S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century. 1b207d990733aaf1: Nearby stores might not actually win out with extra shoppers if a Walmart shutters. Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty ImagesShoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate. Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road. But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger? We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026. This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor. The benefits of an anchor Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business. Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect: Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants. Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop. But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest. What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes. A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area. This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough. Developers often place an anchor store in a bigger retail center to attract more foot traffic overall, which in turn goes to other stores. David Cooper/Toronto Star via Getty Images What happened after a Walmart closed We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open. We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes. That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared. In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally. Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand. Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales. Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed. These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure. Why a store closing can become a neighborhood shock A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores. That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits. For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s. Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area. Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic. 85e2d6b966948461: Pro-monarchists celebrate after the 1953 Iranian coup. Intercontinentale/AFP via Getty Images“Very little gets into, or out of, Iran!” President Donald Trump claimed on Nov. 8, 2026, in a social media post that also lauded “history’s greatest Naval Blockade.” It followed the unveiling of Task Force Iron Gate – the Trump administration’s latest plan to isolate the Iranian economy in a bid to coerce the government in Tehran to bend to Washington’s will. At the same time, Trump has suggested that a return to open war with Iran is “highly unlikely.” From my perspective as an expert on Iran’s relations with the wider world, I believe that the U.S. war in Iran – now into its ninth month – is increasingly resembling an earlier episode of Iranian-Western conflict. In the early 1950s, the British imposed a two-year blockade and embargo against Iran after Iran’s then-prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, nationalized the country’s U.K.-controlled oil industry. These efforts culminated in a 1953 British- and American-backed plot to stir up protest in Iran and eventually overthrow Mossadegh. Seventy-three years later, many of those themes – oil, economic coercion, political intervention – ring true again. Trump’s stated and shifting justifications for the war include imminent threat preemption and nuclear nonproliferation. Yet his main motivations seem to be choosing Iran’s leader and controlling its oil. Having failed to achieve this through direct military force, Trump’s main means for achieving the objectives are now a naval blockade and economic isolation – much like the British some seven decades earlier. But there the analogy may end. Unlike during the Mossadegh era, Iran has shown it can fight back against foreign intervention and coercive economic actions through asymmetric warfare and economic disruption. From oil nationalization … In March 1951, one month before becoming prime minister and while serving as a parliamentary representative, Mossadegh persuaded the Iranian parliament to pass legislation that nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. While popular with many Iranians, who perceived it as a long overdue measure to reclaim the nation’s independence and control its wealth, the move was considered by the British a breach of contract and a theft of its largest overseas asset. The U.K. filed complaints with the newly created United Nations Security Council. But in July of that year, negotiations stalled and tensions escalated between Mossadegh – now the prime minister – and the British. Economic coercion began with the British obstructing Iran’s oil sales by informing Iranian tankers that their receipts – issued when cargo is loaded on board – would not be accepted on the international market. In August, the U.K. stepped up the campaign by imposing a naval blockade against Iran. In the process, they intercepted oil tankers off the Persian coast and prevented Iran from exporting petroleum to other countries. The British also prohibited the export of key commodities to Iran – such as sugar and steel – and froze Iranian bank accounts and assets in the U.K. That same month, the U.K. evacuated its British technicians and closed Anglo-Iranian Oil Company refineries and other installations in the city of Abadan. Mossadegh and his government assumed they could replace the technicians with those from other countries while training Iranians to fill the void. However, through legal threats and agreements, the British convinced other international oil companies in the United States and Europe, except Italy, to refrain from sending personnel. … to Operation Ajax Due to the British blockade and embargo, Iran’s petroleum production declined by about 96% and its oil income to almost zero between 1950 and 1952. At the same time, foreign oil companies like British Petroleum and Saudi Aramco doubled their production to offset the economic impact to the U.K. and the world of reduced or nonexistent production and exports from Iran. Amid the economic crisis, Mossadegh’s inability to alleviate poverty, among other issues, caused his political coalition to fracture and fueled the British and American propaganda campaign against him ahead of his overthrow in Operation Ajax on Aug. 19, 1953. A year later, the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, consolidated power and signed an oil agreement with the British. In it, Iran’s share of the profits increased slightly, while an overwhelming majority of between 75% and 79% continued to be claimed by British and American companies. In exchange, the British lifted the blockade and enabled Iran to resume exporting oil on the international market. The difference of deterrence The U.K.’s campaign to pressure Iran and oust its leader contains parallels with the current conflict. Now, just as then, a Western power is hoping to bring Iranian leadership to its knees – and encourage widespread anti-government protests – through coercive economic actions. But contrary to the 1950s, Tehran today is better placed to deter its foreign adversary. While Washington has drastically degraded Iran’s conventional military capabilities, including its air force and navy, Tehran has effectively employed drones, missiles and proxies to repeatedly strike U.S. assets in the region. Back in the 1950s, Iran had no network of sympathetic regional militias like it has today, and it lacked the sufficient technology to hit back at a conventionally superior military. Iran can also counter economic measures. Since the war began in February 2026, Tehran and its partners have continuously targeted the tanker traffic and civilian and energy infrastructure of the Arab Gulf states. Consequently, it has caused Gulf kingdoms to rethink remaining under the U.S. security umbrella and diversify defense partnerships to include other powers inside and outside the region. A crude oil tanker unloads cargo in Greece after departing Fujairah Anchorage, a major Middle Eastern oil export hub outside the Strait of Hormuz. Nicolas Koutsokostas/NurPhoto via Getty Images Iran has also asserted control, to different degrees, over the critical choke points of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait in cooperation with the Houthis in Yemen. By attacking the Arab Gulf states and disrupting commercial vessels in the region, Iran has driven up the price of oil and other commodities and exerted economic and political pressure on the United States and other countries. And while the U.S. sanctions and other measures have exacerbated the formidable economic challenges facing Iran that predated the war – record currency devaluation, runaway inflation and contracted growth – the regime in Tehran has seemingly weathered the serious social unrest that transpired right before the conflict, during which thousands of protesters and other citizens took to the streets and were killed by the security forces. Unlike Mossadegh, the current leaders of Iran have had decades to build up a resilience to outside pressure. And while it took two years of economic pressure to push Mossadegh from power, years of sanctions have to date failed to bring Iran’s Islamic Republic to its knees. There is no guarantee that increasing the pressure now will change that. Eric Lob is affiliated with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

7daf498ddabc4da7: PARIS (France), Nov 11 — French police have searched two Paris properties linked to Mohamed Al-Fayed, the Ritz and Villa Windsor, as part of an investigation into an alleged international network trafficking women for the late billionaire, prosecutors told AFP today.

The operations in mid-October at the swanky hotel and the onetime residence of the former king of England represent a development in a probe launched in 2025 to track down accomplices of Fayed and his brother, Salah Al-Fayed.
The Paris prosecutor’s office told AFP individuals had been held for questioning in the investigation and authorities were analysing computers, phones and other digital media.

Along with the searches and evidence-gathering operations at the emblematic Paris addresses, authorities also investigated Mohamed Al-Fayed’s former property on the French Riviera, the Castel Sainte-Therese in Saint-Tropez.

The Egyptian-born tycoon, who died aged 94 in 2023 with no charges brought against him despite multiple complaints, owned the Ritz as well as the London luxury department store Harrods and the Fulham football club.

He had lived at the Villa Windsor, the well-known former British royal residence in the Bois de Boulogne in western Paris that the Al-Fayed family had made their favourite holiday home in the French capital.
Victims cited the locations as the sites of alleged abuse by Fayed.

The Paris prosecutor’s office in the summer of 2025 opened an investigation into claims of aggravated human trafficking, procuring prostitutes and rape in a bid to shed light on the alleged network and track down accomplices.
The alleged trafficking ring is believed to have extended into France, particularly at the Ritz and on the French Riviera.
France’s anti-human trafficking unit has interviewed at least five complainants as part of the investigation.
Sources close to the case told AFP that the recent searches and detentions for questioning were carried out in connection with the probe.
‘Courage to speak out’
The investigation is running parallel to British proceedings linked to the wide-ranging scandal over alleged sexual abuse involving Mohamed Al-Fayed.

As of mid-October, 163 victims have reported allegations to the police of sexual assault, rape, sexual exploitation and human trafficking in relation to Fayed. London’s Metropolitan Police acknowledges they are aware of many more who have not come forward.
The Met have been heavily criticised by many survivors of Al-Fayed’s alleged abuse for being slow to grasp the scale of the alleged offences and investigate accordingly.
The London force has questioned seven people suspected of enabling Mohamed Al-Fayed, but none has been charged.
French and British investigators have also been exchanging information and the prosecutor’s office said UK authorities were present during the recent operations.

“Every month, new victims from around the world overcome their fears and find the courage to speak out about what they endured. And we continue to uncover, with astonishment, the scale of Mohamed and Salah Al-Fayed’s actions,” lawyers Eva Joly, Caroline Joly and Agathe Barril, who represent several complainants, told AFP.

“We are, however, only halfway through the investigations,” they added. “But the testimony already points to an organisation in which their immense personal wealth and business empire were allegedly mobilised in the service of their sexual predation: a mechanism devised with cold calculation and meticulous care.”

The management of the Ritz, the famed five-star hotel on Paris’s Place Vendome, told AFP it “does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour”, adding that it was ready “to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities”. — AFP
20d1c60b1d597293: KUALA LUMPUR: Former prime minister Najib Razak has arrived at his home in Jalan Langgak Duta, Taman Duta here where he will serve out the remainder of his six-year jail term for his SRC International conviction.
The former Umno president, who begins his house arrest today following a revised High Court order issued earlier today, arrived at his residence in a prisons department vehicle at 9.29pm.
Some supporters who were gathered outside greeted Najib with shouts of “Bossku”, a nickname made popular after Barisan Nasional fell from power in 2018.
Vehicles ferrying his family members and lawyer, Shafee Abdullah, were also seen arriving earlier.
Najib will be under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028.

Najib was jailed in August 2022 after the Federal Court upheld his conviction for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving RM42 million in SRC funds. He was sentenced to 12 years in jail and fined RM210 million.
In January 2024, then Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah halved Najib's prison sentence and reduced his fine to RM50 million as part of a royal pardon.

In September this year, the current Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim, granted Najib a further conditional pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028.
This was subject to Najib paying the RM50 million fine and complying with other stipulated conditions.

Last Friday, the High Court issued an order of discharge on payment of fine but the Attorney-General's Chambers raised an issue with the document, questioning the accuracy of the terminology and legal provisions used in it.
This afternoon, the High Court voided the initial order and issued a fresh order to allow Najib to begin his house arrest today.

0a7f24e7607a8498: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar.

The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted.
"Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks.

The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited.
Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit.

The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine.

The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited.

The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days, including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight.

That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess.

Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually by heading to Chrome's Settings menu and selecting About Chrome. With attackers already making use of the vulnerability, it's probably worth doing that sooner rather than waiting for Chrome to get around to it. ®

Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
—Grace Huckins

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.

“We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it.
The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape.
