8f873d564b72118e: Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware group BYOD.
Vanderbilt announced on Monday morning that it was dealing with "an active cybersecurity incident," and that the fallout may affect university devices, systems, and cloud-based services.

The Nashville-based university initially told students and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi. It warned them to watch for unexpected prompts, altered files or permissions, unfamiliar applications, and unsolicited authentication requests.
Campus computers reportedly began playing an audio threat attributed to BYOD. Student newspaper The Vanderbilt Hustler cited posts on campus social network Fizz showing the message.

"You have been compromised by BYOD," the recording said. "We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one."
By Monday evening, Vanderbilt had restored access to campus Wi-Fi, but warned that access to most systems remains restricted.

"We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university," it said. "Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation."
Students were told to attend classes as scheduled on Tuesday and contact instructors about flexibility on coursework deadlines. Staff were instructed to report to work normally.
Vanderbilt's Athletics department said that its ticketing system was unavailable, and that students were unable to claim tickets for the college's football game against Alabama on Saturday.
BYOD claimed responsibility for the attack on Vanderbilt on Monday, along with extensive data theft.
"If you could not tell already, your databases are locked [and] we have your entire estate and research data," it said via its leak site.
"Over 1 million SSNs, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, student and employee records, full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess."
Vanderbilt has not confirmed BYOD's claims about the extent of its access or the data allegedly stolen.
BYOD may be a familiar name to some. The group previously claimed attacks on the University of New Mexico and Trump Mobile's customer database.
BYOD also claimed responsibility on Monday for an attack on Texas Health and Human Services. The agency has not publicly confirmed an incident and did not immediately respond to our questions. ®
4668ffcb5b4538a3: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible.

Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize.
Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?

EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted:

“We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.”
A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem

As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on.
Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience.

That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions.
Beyond optimization

For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways.

The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential.

Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness.
Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology

Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT.

“The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste.
Innovation happens at the boundaries

EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies.

Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work.

“Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production.
Building a technology platform

A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications.

Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point.
“The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains.
That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing.
The future of materials companies

The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise.

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible.

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives.

The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030. Beyond producing low-CO2, chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum.
The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today?
The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on.

e4c8ab71581719cc: Between 12 and 13 million UK smart meters could stop working properly when 2G and 3G networks are switched off by 2033, and replacing them all is likely to cost around £4 billion ($5.3 billion).
Smart meters have long been a controversial topic thanks to the British government's botched rollout of the technology; they were supposed to be fitted into 80 percent of households by 2020.
But numerous delays and technical hitches, such as consumers finding their meter stopped being smart if they switched energy supplier, hindered progress.

Now, a report from connectivity biz Wirepas, "The European Connectivity Trilemma," shows that it isn't just Brits who have problems, but that other European countries also have their share of smart meter issues and that no two countries have adopted the same approach.

The UK's issues center on the fact that early meters used 2G or 3G cellular connections to transmit energy usage back to the supplier. These continued to be fitted until 4G versions began arriving at the end of 2024, the report says.
This issue was covered by The Register back in 2023, and again in 2024.

However, the government had already announced measures to phase out 2G and 3G networks by 2033 several years earlier, back in 2021, so it was known that any meters being fitted would have a limited lifespan.

In fact, 3G services have now already been withdrawn by the networks, and they all plan to phase out 2G ahead of the 2033 deadline. BT/EE will begin closing its network from May 2029, VMO2 will start the same summer, and Vodafone aims to switch off in spring 2030.

The report claims the UK now faces two substantial areas of expenditure as a result. The first covers newer, second generation (SMETS2) meters, where only the communications module needs swapping out, but even this is likely to cost £1.3 to £1.4 billion (c $1.7 to $1.9 billion) before the hardware cost of each new hub is even factored in.

The other is for an estimated 7 million older, first-generation (SMETS1) meter installations, which have the cellular comms hard-wired in, so the whole meter typically needs replacing. The report authors estimate this will cost another £2.1 billion to £2.45 billion ($2.8 billion to $3.3 billion), at an indicative replacement cost of £300 to £350 per installation.
This results in the estimated £4 billion in gross replacement costs, which will ultimately feed into household energy bills, adding to the very costs the government is currently trying to reduce.
We asked the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), which oversees smart meters, for comment. A spokesperson said:

"Smart meters are already helping millions of consumers manage their energy and save money on bills," they told The Reg. "The transition to 4G is a planned upgrade that will continue to deliver the benefits that smart meters already provide to households and industry."

While some of these older meters would naturally have been due for replacement as part of normal asset renewal cycles, the cell network shutdown makes the replacement program unavoidable and dictates when much of the expenditure must occur.

According to the report, the SMETS2 replacement largely applies to central and southern Britain, as second-gen meters in the north use a long-range radio network and are not subject to the 2G/3G cut-off. However, the issue of older SMETS1 meters applies nationwide.

Wirepas' interest in all of this is that it specializes in IoT connectivity and is pushing NR+ as a solution to the issue. Based on the DECT-2020 New Radio standard developed by the European Telecommunication Standards Institute (ETSI), this is designed to be scalable and operates in the license-exempt and globally available 1.9GHz part of the spectrum.

When 4G technology reaches the end of its life, (which isn't likely to happen until the 2040s, and there is no planned date) the UK's smart meters will need to be replaced once again, the report asserts. However, this is sufficiently far in the future that it is unlikely to trouble policymakers anytime soon. ®

e15883ed7bcf6381: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation.

They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification.

In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, thereby validating the design of libsignal's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy.

In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean.

The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review.
The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness.

"It's a system that is fundamentally built for human AI collaboration," said Swarat Chaudhuri, research scientist at Google DeepMind and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, in an interview with The Register.

Traditionally, said Chaudhuri, you start proving theorems with well-defined problems formulated by a mathematician that get submitted to an AI agent for proof. In this case, the researchers had to figure out what to prove.

"In formal methods, we always had this belief that verification is the hard bit," he said. "There's thirty or forty years of work on how to scale up verification. Now we are able to do that. So now the question is what are we verifying? … That process is fundamentally human-in-the-loop, but we devised a process of trying to scale it up to the extent possible with AI."

As Chaudhuri and his colleagues note in their research paper, "AlphaProof Code: Verifying Signal’s Security at the Machine-Code Level," formal verification used to require heroic efforts. Formally verifying the seL4 microkernel took 20 person-years, while developing the verified CompCert C compiler took six years.
AlphaProof Code, they believe, can drastically reduce the cost of formal verification, though their Signal work still took four weeks for a team of five people and "quite a few tokens."

"The dream is definitely to scale this up," said Chaudhuri. "So you know there's been this rise in offensive AI capabilities, right? There are a lot of insecure systems around the world, and they're going to be exploited.

"So what we really need to do is to apply this kind of technology to code at large all over the world and figure out what is it that you want to guard against? How do you write those properties, how do we specify those properties? That's going to be super important, but we have to figure that out."

Pointing to a related DeepMind project, AlphaProof Nexus, which is focused on mathematics, Chaudhuri said the next step is to apply this technology during the software design process – not just to cryptographic protocols but code in general.

"We really believe that the next frontier is not going to be proof but specification in this kind of research," he said. "And so that's why we took on this domain where that was actually a hard problem. And I think that we have some really good insights now about how to go about this, although not the last word by any means." ®

7f5b2df7ca43170b: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — For some Malaysian Chinese youths, deciding where to study after secondary school is not simply a matter of choosing a course or university.
Most of these choices are made through weighing how secure they feel about their chances of getting into their preferred programme.

In a research conducted by IMAN Research, they found that uncertainty over public university admissions, differences between pre-university pathways and concerns about access to certain courses had influenced how some the research participants approached their education.

In its recently published report, Kami Orang Sini Juga: Chinese Youths and Democratic Belonging — The Politics of Pragmatism and Fairness, draws on interviews with 116 Malaysian Chinese youths aged between 18 and 35 across Peninsular Malaysia.

The study found that education was one of the areas where participants’ perceptions of fairness were particularly shaped by their own experiences, expectations and accounts they had heard from others.
Some participants described choosing private education or overseas study rather than applying through the public university admission system.

One interviewee, for instance, went directly to a private university without applying through the Unit Pusat Universiti (UPU), citing concerns within the family about the chances of securing a place through the public route.
Another participant who wanted to study medicine declined an offer to pursue biotechnology and instead went to China.
The report describes these decisions as examples of how young people may seek alternatives when public pathways appear uncertain.

However, it also makes an important distinction between barriers participants personally experienced, obstacles they anticipated and accounts they had heard from family members or their wider community.
These are not the same kinds of evidence, and the researchers cautioned against treating every disappointing outcome or decision not to apply as proof of discrimination.
Matriculation and UPU are not the same
The research found that there was a recurring source of confusion among participants — the relationship between the matriculation quota and university admissions through UPU.
The report clarifies that the 90 per cent Bumiputera quota applies to entry into matriculation, not to UPU’s university selection formula.
UPU ranks applicants from STPM, matriculation and other equivalent qualifications using 90 per cent academic marks and 10 per cent co-curricular marks.
Candidates are considered according to merit, programme requirements, available places and their course preferences.
The report said the UPU pathway itself does not have an ethnic quota system.
However, the researchers noted that differences between Sijil Tinggi Persekolahan Malaysia (STPM) and matriculation could still raise questions about fairness.
STPM generally takes one and a half years, while the main matriculation programme takes one year.
The two pathways also use different assessment structures.
How are they different?
STPM students may progress through school, zone, district, state and national competitions, while matriculation students compete within a structure centred on inter-college competitions.

Citing figures that showed 16 per cent of matriculation students achieved a cumulative grade point average of 4.0, compared with 3.09 per cent of STPM students, the researchers suggest these differences be examined when considering how students from the two pathways are assessed

For popular courses such as medicine, pharmacy and dentistry at public universities, matriculation students accounted for more than 97 per cent of places in 2023, while STPM students made up less than 3 per cent, according to figures cited in the report.
These figures were used to illustrate differences in outcomes between the pathways, rather than establish that any individual applicant had been unfairly treated.
When students look for alternatives
The report found that family resources played an important role in determining whether young people could pursue alternatives when they felt uncertain about public education pathways.
Some could afford private universities or overseas study, while others had fewer options.
This meant that the ability to work around perceived barriers was not equally available to everyone.
The researchers also noted that concerns inherited from parents or community members could influence decisions even before a student applied for a place.
In such cases, these Chinese youths people might rule out a pathway based on what they had heard about the system, rather than on a direct experience of rejection.
The report recommends that the government make university admissions criteria, selection mechanisms and intake data more transparent and accessible.
It also calls for students to be given clearer information about how different pre-university qualifications are assessed and how they affect university options.

The researchers said differences in co-curricular opportunities between STPM and matriculation should also be reviewed, alongside clearer pathways for students holding the Unified Examination Certificate who wish to enter public universities.
Rather than redesigning the entire pre-university system, the report suggests addressing specific areas where the students face uncertainty or unequal opportunities.

Its broader concern is that when students cannot clearly understand how public education pathways work, they may make decisions based on assumptions, family experiences or perceived limitations — potentially narrowing their choices before they have fully explored them.

aa7da1e6d9c493bb: PETALING JAYA: MISC Bhd’s proposal to acquire and privatise Yinson Holdings Bhd via a consortium would increase its financial risk, a research house said.
CGS International warned that the energy infrastructure group's heavy gearing leaves shareholders particularly “exposed to project execution risks”.
“Yinson is very highly geared, and its operational execution needs to be almost perfect for its shareholders to secure positive returns,” said CGS in a research note.

It put Yinson’s net gearing at 1.1 times as at July 31, rising to 3.1 times under its assessment if perpetual securities and redeemable convertible preference shares (RCPS) were reclassified from equity to debt.
It said, though, that this financial structure could amplify returns from Yinson’s future contract wins, it also “accentuates the risk to shareholders”.

A slowdown in awards for floating production, storage and offloading (FPSO) vessels could also delay those gains, said CGS, while questioning whether paying cash was the best way for Petronas-controlled MISC to expand its offshore business.

Last Friday, MISC together with Yinson’s founding Lim family and the Employees Provident Fund (EPF) proposed to take Yinson private at RM2.50 a share, a 10.6% premium to its closing price of RM2.26 on Nov 6.
The acquisition of the remaining 55.2% stake in Yinson will entail a cash consideration of RM4.03 billion, valuing the group at RM7.31 billion.

The transaction will be undertaken through MY Offshore Holdings Sdn Bhd (MYOH), in which MISC and Yinson Legacy Sdn Bhd (YLSB), the investment vehicle of Yinson executive chairman Lim Han Weng, will each hold a 41.46% stake, while EPF will retain an effective 17.07% stake.

MISC will inject RM3.03 billion into MYOH to acquire the shares while YLSB, which owns 27.73% of Yinson, will transfer its stake to MYOH and contribute the remaining RM1 billion in cash. EPF will only roll over its shares. The acquisition is expected to be completed in the second half of 2027.

MISC plans to finance about three-quarters of its RM3.03 investment through new borrowings amounting to RM2.27 billion, with the remainder funded internally. At end-June, the oil and gas shipping company had RM7.2 billion in cash, deposits and bank balances, against total borrowings of RM12.96 billion.
CGS maintained its “reduce” recommendation on MISC with a RM7.58 target price. The stock fell 2 sen or 0.25% to RM7.99 today, valuing it at RM35.67 billion.

Meanwhile, TA Research said the acquisition is expected to increase MISC’s pro forma gearing from 0.36 times to 0.43 times, reflecting the additional borrowings required to fund approximately 75% of its RM3 billion investment.

It noted the additional debt will raise MISC’s financing commitments, with the returns from Yinson needing to sufficiently compensate for the associated funding costs. The transaction is also unlikely to materially enhance MISC's near-term earnings, the research house added.

Analysts agree that MISC’s investment provides it with exposure to Yinson’s established FPSO platform alongside an offshore contracted revenue backlog of approximately US$19.3 billion (RM78.3 billion).

Yinson was founded by Lim, 73, and his wife Bah Kim Lian in 1984, as a lorry transport company before diversifying into the oil and gas sector. It is now one of the world’s biggest providers of FPSO vessels, which are used to extract and store crude oil.

7156c96ea3142782: The European Union has dragged IBM, Atos, and Leonardo into court over years of delays to its troubled €212 million smart border system, which finally went live after missing a string of deadlines and leaving travelers stuck in airport queues.
The lawsuit dates back to December 22, 2025, when eu-LISA, the agency behind the EU's fingerprint-and-facial-image border checks for non-EU travelers, filed its claim in an Estonian court.

The lawsuit was buried in eu-LISA's 2025 financial accounts, published in July, with no mention of who was being sued. The Financial Times has since named the three companies after obtaining letters exchanged with the agency.
In a statement to The Register, eu-LISA confirmed it had initiated proceedings "in line with the Agency’s responsibility to protect the EU’s financial interests."

"The proceedings concern the system’s development phase and have no impact on its current operation. EES (entry exit system) is fully operational," the agency said, declining to discuss the ongoing case.

The EES was supposed to be ready in 2022 yet wasn't live until October 2025 and was only fully operational from April. Travelers have since had to contend with hours-long airport queues and fingerprint scanners that reportedly struggle with sweaty fingers. Behind the scenes, things weren't going much better, with the consortium and eu-LISA spending years arguing over missed deadlines, financial penalties and who was to blame.

IBM Belgium and Atos Belgium were already arguing over penalties back in October 2021, when they disputed a fine from eu-LISA and pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic and other factors beyond their control as reasons for the delays.
By February 2022, the consortium was pushing back against another set of deadlines, warning that the agency's timetable was unrealistic.

"Ignoring reality is not prudent and will not help to achieve the plan," the companies wrote, according to the FT. "On the contrary, working with an unrealistic plan will cause frustration for all stakeholders."
The consortium also criticized eu-LISA's "overall governance," suggesting relations between the two sides had become rather frosty.
The fallout wasn't cheap. The contract had already grown from €142 million to €212 million in 2021, and the delays kept adding to the bill.

In its 2022 accounts [PDF], eu-LISA acknowledged difficulties with the consortium and warned of additional costs, with the setbacks also holding up other EU IT projects. By 2023, it had nearly doubled its annual EES budget to €40 million by diverting funds from elsewhere, partly to cover rising hardware and software maintenance costs.
The FT also reported that IBM agreed in March 2022 to let eu-LISA withhold certain payments while the dispute over damages was resolved.
The original contract expired last year, with a new consortium taking over implementation, although IBM, Atos, and Leonardo remained responsible until August.

The project has attracted scrutiny for more than its ballooning budget. Last year, Atos reportedly used its Moscow office to procure software for the system, raising questions about Russian involvement in sensitive European border infrastructure.

The EU's anti-fraud office, OLAF, found sufficient grounds for further investigation, according to an internal report seen by the FT. However, it referred the matter back to eu-LISA despite describing the agency's initial assessment as insufficient.
Estonia's Harju County Court confirmed that the civil case had been filed, although no hearings have taken place or been scheduled.
IBM and Atos did not respond to The Register's questions.
The EES may finally be up and running, but the argument over who should foot the bill for getting it there looks far from settled. ®

bed4b88baa6fc062: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — When Violet Lee Zi Yi began researching Malaysian Chinese youths, she admitted she initially approached the community with assumptions about its relative economic advantages, resources and access to opportunities.
What she discovered through interviews with these youths across Peninsular Malaysia was a much more complicated picture.

“I initially thought Chinese is a unitary block. It is so different,” Lee said in an interview about the findings of IMAN Research’s report, Kami Orang Sini Juga: Chinese Youths and Democratic Belonging — The Politics of Pragmatism and Fairness.
The report, prepared by Lee and co-researcher Liew Liang Hong, is based on interviews with 116 Malaysian Chinese youths aged between 18 and 35 conducted from August 2025 to April 2026.
It examines Chinese youths on how they understand their identity, navigate opportunities and inequality, and relate to politics and public institutions.

Rather than treating Malaysian Chinese youths as a single political or cultural group, the research found that their experiences were shaped by factors including family history, language, schooling, religion, socioeconomic background and where they grew up.
For some, regional identities such as being Penangite, Johorean or an anak Terengganu were just as important in defining who they were.
“When I started the research, I went into it with a mindset of — apa lagi Cina mahu or what else do the Chinese want?
“I wanted to understand what more Malaysian Chinese youths wanted, so I had assumptions about the community’s relative advantages.
“But the interviews changed my perception. Everyone’s experience is so diverse, so different, and every conversation just added what I had never imagined before,” she said.
One example was how family history could shape identity differently across generations.

Lee said she had not initially considered how being a third-generation Malaysian Chinese could produce a different outlook from being fourth-generation, depending on how grandparents and great-grandparents had spoken about China and their family’s history.
She said these differences emerged naturally during the conversations, illustrating how the research uncovered experiences that the team had not anticipated when designing its questions.
Belonging is not always straightforward
The report found that national identity did not necessarily come at the expense of Chinese cultural identity.
Some participants described themselves primarily as Malaysian, while others considered Malaysian Chinese an inseparable identity.
Others placed strong emphasis on their state or hometown.
For some interviewees from the East Coast, being an anak Terengganu was central to how they described home, even as they recognised restrictions associated with being part of a minority community.

One participant described the distinction between feeling at home and feeling politically restricted, saying: “As a layman I feel I belong, but in politics I feel being restricted, like in Matriculation and fund allocation.”
The report said these feelings could coexist: participants could feel emotionally attached to Malaysia while questioning how public resources and institutions treated different communities.
It also found that everyday interactions could foster a sense of shared Malaysian identity.
Participants spoke positively about ordinary experiences such as eating at mamak restaurants, mixing languages and joining one another’s festivals.

However, the researchers cautioned against romanticising these interactions, noting that cordial relationships did not necessarily translate into deeper understanding or erase concerns about institutional fairness.
The cost of pragmatism
One of the report’s central findings is what it calls “self-cornering” — the tendency to find private ways around perceived problems rather than challenge the institutions behind them.
The report found that some young people responded to uncertainty over public opportunities by working harder, relying on family networks, paying for alternatives or looking overseas.
These decisions could be practical and help individuals secure their futures, but the researchers argued that they also carried wider consequences.

When those with sufficient resources could find private alternatives, the institutions and policies behind their concerns remained unchanged. Those without the means to find alternatives could be left with fewer options.
The report also distinguished between inequality personally experienced by participants, barriers they anticipated and accounts they had heard from family or community members.
It cautioned against treating every disappointing outcome as proof of discrimination, while recognising that inherited accounts could influence how young people assessed their prospects.
Wanting to be heard
Another finding concerned the distance between young people and the organisations or institutions expected to represent them.
Lee said she was struck by how some interviewees did not consider their own opinions valuable simply because they were not politically vocal.
“We wanted to include young people who were not already active in community organisations or political circles, rather than relying mainly on those who were accustomed to speaking publicly.
“Only about 10 to 15 per cent of those recruited were young leaders.

“This was important because young people who were already involved in organisations were often more comfortable expressing their views, while others might not see their own experiences as worth sharing,” she said.
The research team also found that established community leaders could say they wanted younger people to participate, yet were sometimes reluctant to give them meaningful space.
Lee said this could leave young people struggling to find where they could contribute, while older leaders continued to hold the resources and decision-making positions.

She also questioned the narrow definition of success within parts of the community, where financial achievement and professional status could be valued more visibly than civic or political participation.
“Chinese youth are not rewarded socially if you are in politics. Only if you become a politician, you become someone famous, then yes, you’re recognised,” she said.
Those working behind the scenes, she added, were less likely to receive recognition.
Lee said the research also found that some young people wanted to move beyond racialised political thinking but were unsure how to do so.
“They are conditioned in the racial politics. They are conditioned into thinking along the communal lines, but they want to break through that.”
Among the many challenges
She said one challenge for the researchers was to ensure that the findings did not simply reflect the views of the loudest or most visible members of the community.
“Being the loudest did not mean that they have a full understanding of a stipulation on ground,” she said.
Not particularly looking for a solution, Lee said the report is a qualitative research and is not statistically representative of all Malaysian Chinese youths.
“Its findings are intended to provide insight into how the participants understood their experiences, rather than measure how widespread particular views are.

“We actually only included 30 per cent of the data collected, there were just too much data which we thought was better to leave them for further research into specific communities and experiences,” she said.
For Lee, the next step is to create more opportunities for young people from different communities to speak to one another.
She said the responsibility should not fall on young people alone, but also on researchers, the media and civil society organisations to create space for discussion.
For her, the research is ultimately about giving young people more room to think about their place in the country, rather than seeing them only as voters whose views matter during elections.
“This research gets the conversation starting especially for Chinese youths who don’t know where to start, or what to do first,” she said.

432961bd20a01d3c: Britain’s Royal Navy has formally commissioned its first uncrewed boat squadron, operating seaborne drones on front-line operations as part of its “Hybrid Navy” strategy.

The force says the 1st Autonomous Squadron officially entered active service on November 5 at a ceremony in Portsmouth Naval Base. It comprises around 180 personnel, about the same as a Type 23 frigate, split into two watches to enable operations around the clock.

This active squadron replaces Project Beehive, the navy’s experimental program to build a fleet of autonomous and remotely operated vessels, through which it obtained 20 uncrewed boats from UK-based Kraken Technology Group.
The force is understood to be using both Kraken’s K3 Scout, and the SM400 from SYOS Aerospace, known by the Royal Navy as the Rattler.

The K3 Scout is an 8.4 m boat capable of 55 knots and can carry a payload of up to 600 kg. It has a range of up to 650 nautical miles and endurance of up to 7 days. The maker describes it as capable of a range of missions, including anti-ship and anti-submarine to detecting and countering other drones and even casualty evacuation.

The Rattler boat is 7.2 m and has a 500 kg modular bay, with a range of up to 950 nautical miles. It was used last year in a demonstration during which 5 of the uncrewed boats were remotely-piloted to escort patrol ship HMS Tyne and mine countermeasures mothership HMS Stirling Castle

Part of the new squadron’s mission will be to act as pathfinder for drone operations, working on bringing additional types of uncrewed surface vessel (USVs) into fleet service and conducting a range of operations alongside other organizations – both as single vessels and as part of a task group.

The “Hybrid Navy” concept was outlined by First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins earlier this year, who made the case that uncrewed vessels would be vital in filling the gaps left by the Royal Navy’s much depleted surface fleet.

Speaking at the launch of the autonomous squadron, Fleet Commander Vice-Admiral Steve Moorhouse hailed it as an historic occasion, but warned that the seas are becoming more contested, more dangerous and harder to operate in.
“A hybrid navy is about giving our people better tools. It means more reach, more striking power and more options,” he stated.

Last week, the force also launched strike drones from one of its aircraft carriers for the first time. Nyan one-way drones made by BAE Systems were launched from the deck, as well as a Tekever AR5 fixed-wing uncrewed aircraft, the same kind the British Army has selected to replace its troublesome Watchkeeper fleet.

Elsewhere, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it has launched a British-built satellite called Titania into orbit, claiming it “gives the Armed Forces a new pair of eyes in space.” However, the original purpose of the orbiter was understood to be to test high-speed optical communications from low Earth orbit directly to Earth, using laser beams that are harder to intercept than radio links.

Titania is the second satellite in the UK’s growing constellation of military satellites in orbit, following the launch of Tyche in October, and will be operated by UK Space Command as part of the ISTARI* program.
The latter aims to deliver satellites and supporting ground systems to expand space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, the MoD said.
However, while the satellite is British-made, it got into space via an American rocket, riding on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 mission. ®

1412273beae0e596: NEW YORK: A top Federal Reserve official said Tuesday that the US central bank must act swiftly and forcefully to address inflation, signalling plans to back an interest rate hike in December.

"Inflation remains too high," Fed governor Christopher Waller said during an address in London. "Monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2% in the medium term."

The speech came a few hours ahead of the release later Tuesday of key US consumer price inflation (CPI) data for October. Waller, in the speech, said he would consider a double-sized 0.5 percentage point increase in interest rates if the October CPI report shows another significant uptick in pricing pressures.

Waller's statement boosts the likelihood that the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next month will lift interest rates for the second time in three meetings, posing another setback for US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pushed for lower rates and whose Republican Party suffered sweeping defeats in last week's midterm elections.
In September, CPI accelerated to 0.6% on a month-on-month basis, while rising 3.7% on a year-on-year basis, due in part to surging gasoline prices related to the US-Iran war.
Waller, who was appointed by Trump in 2020 to the Fed's seven-member Board of Governors, called the September data "bad", with "no silver lining".

Waller cited inflationary effects from the artificial intelligence buildout and pointed to Fed research that suggests "energy price pressures may pass through to goods and services in a more sustained way than in the past."

"Even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting," Waller said.
But if October pricing dynamics are similar to last month's, "then a stronger policy move may be needed," he said.

"In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take."
e7372b2100ebfac3: Microsoft is retiring its free education email service, leaving schools, colleges, and universities facing new licensing bills if they want to keep students' mailboxes.

The company announced plans last week to retire Office 365 A1, the Student Use Benefit program, and free Exchange Online for Alumni. The changes generally take effect at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028.

Office 365 A1 provides eligible institutions with web-based Office applications, Teams, and email at no charge. Its replacement, Microsoft 365 Education A0, excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also depends on paid faculty licensing and students actively using Windows devices for education.

A spokesperson for the UK's Department for Education told The Register: "We are disappointed that Microsoft has made this decision. However, we are pleased to have successfully negotiated some additional concessions for the UK, giving schools, colleges and universities the time they need to be able to successfully transition to new licensing agreements."

An industry insider said the loss of free Microsoft-hosted email could add thousands to institutions' bills. Another organization noted "significant concerns… around affordability, equitable treatment across the sector, and the longer-term implications of the changes."

A spokesperson for UK education technology body Jisc told The Register that its "focus has been on ensuring that UK education providers are well supported and have sufficient time to assess their options."
"We continue working closely with Microsoft and sector partners to support those discussions and help institutions make informed decisions about their future requirements."

Also being retired are free Exchange Online for Alumni – which lets graduates retain their mailboxes – and the Student Use Benefit, providing student licenses at no additional charge when institutions purchase qualifying faculty licenses. Microsoft plans a paid alumni replacement.

The Windows giant is also changing storage entitlements and introducing Microsoft 365 Education A7, its "most advanced education offering," which adds AI, security, governance, and device-management features.
Asked why it was removing those services from the free tier, Microsoft framed the overhaul as a response to institutions' changing needs.

A spokesperson told The Register: "Education institutions are evaluating AI, security, privacy, governance, and teaching and learning as connected priorities rather than separate technology decisions.

"Microsoft is updating the portfolio now to provide a clearer path from foundational access to advanced capabilities, while enabling institutions to adopt technology according to their needs and readiness. This evolution reflects both the value Microsoft 365 Education has gained since the last pricing change nearly a decade ago and the structure of the new portfolio.

"Microsoft's broader goal is not technology adoption for its own sake. It is to support AI and digital experiences that strengthen learning, preserve educator judgment and give institutions the controls they need to manage data, privacy, and responsible use."

Office 365 A1 stopped accepting new web-direct orders on November 5, 2026, with partner-channel sales ending on May 1, 2027. Retirement is scheduled for January 1, 2028, but existing agreements remain valid through their current terms. Institutions that need continued service must move to replacement licenses at the applicable renewal or contract expiry. ®

31908bd5800c5bf4: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 — The High Court has directed the Court Registrar to issue a new order that would finally allow Datuk Seri Mohd Najib Abdul Razak to serve the remaining sentence of his first corruption conviction at home.
High Court Judge Datuk Aslam Zainuddin issued the new warrant of release after hearing submissions by both Najib’s lawyers and the Deputy Public Prosecutors this afternoon.

At the hearing, Najib’s lead counsel Tan Sri Shafee Abdullah had argued that the court need not issue a new order since the first was already “very clear”.
He alleged even the Prison Department understood the discharge order, was ready to release the former prime minister but “was then told to wait”.

Shafee’s core argument was that the condition to trigger Najib’s release from Kajang Prison and serve home imprisonment - paying the RM50 million - was already met, and that the ensuing order of discharge issued by the High Court Registrar was worded in a way that reflected that.

In a press conference held shortly after the hearing ended, Shafee welcomed the clarification by Judge Aslam even has he maintained his argument that the original order was “solid in substance”, and that all matters regarding the King’s pardon need not be formalised by the judicial system.
“It is good that the court has clarified so that those who apparently found it hard to understand, will now understand,” he said.
Najib, in a light blue baju melayu top with sleeves rolled up, was present at the hearing alongside his daughter Najwa, who was also in a blue floral baju kurung.

Shafee said Najib would likely be home by tonight, after all formal documents have been submitted to Kajang Prison where he would also be briefed about the conditions of his house arrest.
Details of the conditions are still not available to the lawyers for now including on visitation Shafee added.
“I assume you will have to apply, at least initially. Or they may make it easier as there is a post (at Najib’s residence), and they may device some system,” he said.

5c7becfbff02111f: NOVEMBER 10 — When I first read the court order concerning former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak’s release following payment of his RM50 million fine, two thoughts immediately crossed my mind.
My first was that the document was fake. Just look at the heading: Order of discharge on payment of fine.
Then came the second line, which read: In the Tinggi Court of Wilayah Persekutuan.
Where on earth can you find a “Tinggi Court” in Malaysia? Surely, this must be a fake court document.

I shared my observation with a source close to the matter, who insisted that the document was genuine. I remained unconvinced, pointing out further evidence that suggested something was seriously wrong with it.
For one, the document switches between English and Bahasa Melayu, sometimes within the same sentence. Having seen and read court documents before, I found this rather odd and unprofessional.
This brings me to my second observation.

The document appears to have been prepared in a hurry, with typos scattered throughout. Apart from the person who drafted it, I doubt anyone checked or edited its spelling, sentence structure or contents.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Datuk Seri Najib Razak is pictured at the Kuala Lumpur Court Complex, in Kuala Lumpur November 25, 2025. — Picture by Firdaus Latif
Najib’s lawyers, who applied for the order, should have noticed these errors if they bothered to read and check the document. They, too, bear some responsibility for the mistakes and inconsistencies.

Although the document is addressed to the officer-in-charge of Kajang prison, the background information about the prisoner appears to list only one charge under Section 406 of the Penal Code, repeated three times, instead of identifying the three charges under three different Acts.
Even the client’s name is inconsistent, appearing sometimes with “Mohd” and sometimes without it.
But the most puzzling part is the last paragraph in the first column, which reads:

“Sekiranya Dato Seri Najib... tidak mematuhi mana-mana syarat-syarat tersebut, maka Perintah ini adalah terbatal dan Dato Seri Najib... hendaklah secara serta-merta meneruskan baki hukuman di Penjara Kajang atau di mana-mana penjara yang ditetapkan oleh Komisioner Jeneral Penjara. or to Menjalani hukuman baki secara tahanan di rumah yang beralamat di No. 11, Jalan Langgak Duta, Taman Duta...”
The mixing of Bahasa Melayu and English in this paragraph is not only poor but also confusing. A sentence cannot simply begin with the lowercase English word “or” and continue in Bahasa Melayu.
More importantly, how is anyone supposed to interpret a sentence that appears to offer three different options, even when the prisoner has failed to comply with the stipulated terms and conditions?

Does the prisoner still have the option of serving the remainder of his sentence at Kajang prison, being transferred to another prison designated by the commissioner-general of prisons, or serving the remainder of his sentence under house arrest at his own residence?
What sort of court order is that?
If this document is indeed genuine, as my source insists, I fully agree with the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) seeking clarification from the court.
There are simply too many errors, inconsistencies and ambiguities in the document to be ignored.
The attorney-general is right to have identified a potential conflict between the High Court’s order of release and the proposed house-arrest arrangement.

An order of release is intended to release a prisoner from custody. It is not an order to transfer a prisoner from one place of detention to another, even if Najib’s residence has been gazetted as a place of detention.
At the same time, the AGC cannot simply disregard a court order, whether it agrees with its contents or not.
The conflict and confusion may have arisen because Najib’s lawyers applied for and obtained what appears to be a conventional order of release, when his circumstances were anything but conventional.
His situation involved an unprecedented house-arrest arrangement that required a properly drafted and legally unambiguous court order.

This entire ordeal has been compounded by what appears to be the failure of a court official to produce a proper, concise and legally precise document in Bahasa Melayu, with clear terms and specific instructions.
Najib’s lawyers should have recognised this problem from the outset and ensured that the appropriate order was sought.

If the order of release is followed, and the AGC has no lawful grounds to refuse compliance with a court order, the consequence could be that Najib is released from his current detention and becomes liable to begin serving his 15-year prison sentence arising from his 1MDB conviction.
The irony is that this entire ordeal may have been caused by Najib’s own lawyers. It is therefore up to them to take the necessary steps to untangle the legal mess they may have created.
The court has a responsibility to issue a legally correct order, but the lawyers seeking that order have an equally important responsibility to ensure that they ask for the right one.
One thing should be made clear: the confusion and conflict are certainly not the king’s fault, nor should the attorney-general be blamed for seeking clarification.
The attorney general is right to insist that the matter be resolved carefully and in accordance with the law.
Given the public interest and constitutional implications, the AGC is also right to proceed cautiously. The eyes of all Malaysians are on this matter.
Ultimately, the law must prevail. Neither the court, the AGC nor the parties involved can afford to leave the public guessing about what the order actually means.
I believe the king and the Malaysian public would understand the need for such clarification.
What was supposed to be a straightforward court order has now become a full-blown court ordeal.

The tax would have forced around 200 billionaires in the state to cough up five per cent of their total net worth, with the money largely dedicated to helping pay for healthcare.
CNN and CBS News both projected that so-called Proposition 40 would not pass, nearly a week after voters cast ballots on whether to tax the billionaires.
With the highest population of any US state, California is notoriously slow at counting votes.

The proposal was unveiled to fanfare in California, a state that would be the world’s fourth largest economy if it were a country, but one in which there is a yawning gulf between the haves and the have-nots.

But the tax already appeared to be headed for defeat last week, with about 60 per cent of votes counted on Wednesday showing that “No” was leading by 55.6 per cent to 44.4 per cent.

“Significant changes rarely move in a straight line,” Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph E. Stiglitz said in a statement sent to AFP by the International Capital Tax Commission before yesterday’s projections.
“Prop 40 put a tax on billionaire wealth on the ballot in the United States for the first time,” he added.
Advocates calculated the one-off tax would raise about US$100 billion (RM405 billion) which would be used to fund a public healthcare system that has been hit by Trump’s budget cuts.
Opponents of the ballot measure, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, raised hundreds of millions of dollars to defeat the idea, arguing it would push the wealthy to leave California.
“No” campaign commercials warning about the loss of future tax revenues if billionaires desert the state played wall-to-wall across TV stations in California in the run-up to the vote.
Outgoing Governor Gavin Newsom, who is widely expected to make a run for the White House in 2028, had said he would vote no.
California has previously voted three times this decade on a wealth tax, rejecting it every time. — AFP

4f02c191dd33421c: Sean Gallup / Getty ImagesJensen Huang, the chief executive and co-founder of chipmaking company Nvidia, recently admitted to an extramarital affair. However, it’s not just a tabloid story: the woman involved, Alice Huang, has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. Computer chips – specifically the chips used to produce and run artificial intelligence (AI) systems – have become a key front in the United States’ rivalry with China for geopolitical power and influence. The most powerful chips are needed for the most advanced AI, and the US has tried to maintain its edge over China by restricting access to those chips. While the Chinese government rejects claims of espionage, Alice Huang has reportedly been under investigation by the US for years. So what’s so special about Nvidia? What’s in it for China? And if Jensen Huang goes down, what else could go down with him? The world’s biggest AI chip company Nvidia is the world’s biggest supplier of the high-end chips used for AI and data centres, with some estimates putting its market share over 80%. The now multi-trillion-dollar company got its start making chips called graphic processing units (GPUs), used largely for video games. However, these chips – and their successors – turned out to be ideal for the kind of number-crunching needed for training and using AI models. Other companies such as Google and AMD have tried to make chips that can compete with Nvidia for speed and efficiency, however neither has been able to displace Nvidia from its dominance of the AI market. Read more: What is a GPU? An expert explains the chips powering the AI boom, and why they’re worth trillions Why China may be interested As a consequence, Nvidia has played a key role in the US government’s strategy to stall China’s development of AI. Sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to China have been restricted since 2022 – though the restrictions were somewhat relaxed last year. However, Chinese enterprises have repeatedly tested the boundaries of US sanctions. Southeast Asian companies including Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s former employer, have been accused of buying up Nvidia chips and exporting them into China. Jensen Huang has lobbied intently for a relaxation of US chip export restrictions, which is being seen in a new light after the revelation of his relationship with Alice Huang. Skipping the sanctions Trade records indicate over US$3 billion in chips crossed from Singapore to China in a single year, alongside similar volumes from Malaysia. Selling access to banned Nvidia chips to Chinese companies has also become a growth industry. Nvidia’s value has soared with the AI boom. However, its share price has fallen after the disclosure of the Huang incident, with some analysts asking whether the company propped up sales figures by ignoring sanctions. It has also been reported that an Nvidia executive leaned on US officials to halt an investigation into the firm’s relationship with Megaspeed. Regulatory impact Nvidia’s share price tumbled after the affair was revealed. Now the company is reportedly under criminal investigation. At the same time, US technology regulators are mobilising, with Congress requesting Jensen Huang explain his interactions with Alice Huang, and how Nvidia protects itself against foreign espionage. If Nvidia is forced to guarantee its chips don’t enter China, its sales pipeline may grind to a halt. And if Nvidia hits trouble, the financial impacts could be much wider. The AI sector is notorious for the amount of circular financing going on – where companies invest in their own suppliers or customers. Nvidia is a key player in this loop. Investors are already fretting over whether the enormous amounts of money sunk into AI can ever return profits. While leading AI model builders Anthropic and OpenAI are moving toward public listings or fresh funding rounds, both face harsh reality checks. OpenAI has delayed its own planned stock market listing, while Anthropic’s expected share market listing is rumoured to face a “junk bond” rating, meaning it’s a high-risk investment. Data centre firms too are losing value as they face community pushback and soaring energy costs. Governance crisis So what now? Clearly Nvidia faces a crisis, with a backlash against AI and data centres sweeping the US, US investigators looking at it closely, and the company’s own board of directors investigating its chief executive. On top of this, Nvidia has been inseparable from Jensen Huang’s personal brand for decades – and that brand is now somewhat tarnished. Until now, investors have supported the company, and Jensen, as visionary underwriters of the entire AI ecosystem. If that changes, or the company otherwise loses its way, a shortage of GPUs may be the least of the AI industry’s problems. 8c4f85be22873ce3: Au Kam San's international legal representative called the trial a ‘sham’ with ‘manufactured allegations’
Originally published on Global Voices
Au Kam San. Photo from Au Kam San's Facebook page.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Chinese territory of Macau recorded its first conviction under the city’s national security law on November 6, 2026, sentencing 69-year-old former lawmaker Au Kam San to 12.5 years in prison. The Macau Court of First Instance tried the case behind closed doors, and international observers and rights groups have criticized the verdict, calling it a “bogus prosecution” that included “serious violations of his right to a fair trial.” The case raises broader questions about how justice is carried out in Macau, and whether its courts offer a fair, open way to challenge the state.

Au served in Macau’s legislature for over 20 years and remained an outspoken current affairs commentator after his retirement in 2021. He was convicted on one count of subverting state power, three counts of contacting foreign organizations to endanger national security, and one count of violating confidentiality.
According to the court’s statement, the closed-door trial was held on September 16 and 18. Au was prosecuted under Macau’s domestic security law, enacted on March 3, 2009, and tightened in 2023.

He was accused of cooperating with hostile foreign organizations to collect and disseminate “numerous political propositions that were clearly permeated with [the intent of] subversion of state power” and to assist in the collection and dissemination of false information that intended to incite hatred against the central government, overthrow and undermine the fundamental national system established by the Chinese Constitution, cause foreign countries to take hostile actions against China and Macau, and disrupt the Macau Chief Executive election in 2024.
Au’s family members, several media outlets, and dozens of citizens attended the court’s public sentencing.

Au’s wife, Cheng Miu-shan, responded to the sentencing with an open letter, stating that the closed-door hearing and public sentencing were politically motivated and a baseless persecution to humiliate and smear her husband’s character.
Au’s daughter, Cherry Au, defended her father’s innocence in her interview with UK-based media outlet, the Independent:

“What saddens me the most is seeing him being portrayed as a villain by the very government that he served for so many years,” she said. “I hope people remember the person they knew throughout his career, the reason why they placed their trust in him and elected him time and again. Right now he is facing profound injustice. I hope those who remember his years of service will stand by him.”

Au Kam San has been detained since his arrest in July 2025. He was initially charged with three counts of “subverting state power,” three counts of “establishing contacts with organizations, groups or individuals outside the Macau Special Administrative Region to commit acts that endanger national security,” and one count of “violating confidentiality.” The court reduced the subversion charge to one count after the closed-door hearing.

After the public sentencing, the court issued a press release stressing that it appointed a lawyer to defend Au and that during the trial, Au did not dispute most of the facts and acknowledged that his collusion with and conspiracy with multiple overseas organizations constituted a crime.

It also pointed out that Au did not stop colluding with foreign and overseas organizations to subvert state power after the 2023 amendment of Macau national security law. The amendment has expanded the definition of subversive acts from “violent means” to “any illegal means,” to more closely align with Hong Kong’s 2020 version of national security law.
However, Au’s daughter told the press that her father had been barred from contacting his family and accessing a private lawyer to represent him in court.

Michael Polak, director of Justice Abroad, who has represented Au to submit an official complaint to the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, called Au’s trial a “sham” with “manufactured allegations” which brought Macau “in line with the most repressive state around the world, where the executive has the power to imprison those with whom it disagrees, with no semblance of a proper, fair legal process.”

In a statement following Au’s public sentencing, Polak also criticized that the private “hearing” had prevented any scrutiny of the Macao Authorities’ so-called evidence, thus creating a scenario where they could present anything, or nothing at all, to the Court and a conviction was inevitable.

So far, the public has not had any information about which foreign organizations, groups, or individuals Au Kam San conspired with to endanger national security and what distorted information he had spread to incite hatred against the Macau government, or undermine China’s socialist system.
The EU also issued a statement criticizing the conviction as “the erosion of political pluralism and freedom of speech” in Macau. It also expressed regret concerning the closed-door trial:
“We regret that access for the public, press and diplomats was restricted. After his arrest on July 30, 2025, Au Kam San had spent almost one year in incommunicado detention.”
Given that Au holds Portuguese citizenship, Polak called on Portugal and the EU to press for his release.

Au Kam San, a retired school teacher, is a prominent pro-democracy activist. After the 1989 pro-democracy movement, along with other pro-democracy figures such as António Ng Kuok Cheong, he established the “Macau Democratic Development Joint Committee” to “respond to the Chinese democratic movement and promote the democratic development of Macau.” They organized and participated in annual activities to commemorate China’s June 4, 1989, Tiananmen Square protests and massacre, until 2021, after the Macau authorities banned the Tiananmen vigil co-organized by Au, claiming that the event would incite state subversion.

Au started his public service career as a Macau municipal councilor from 1993 to 2001. In the first Legislative Council election after Macau’s reunification with China in 1999, Au and Ng formed a political team, “Democratic New Macau,” which won the race with 21 percent of the vote in their constituency. He was re-elected four times until 2021, when he announced his retirement. That year, the Election Committee disqualified 21 candidates from running in the legislative race, citing the Macau Court of Appeal ruling that supported Macau’s decision to ban commemoration of the June 4th Tiananmen Incident as subversive.
Written by Global Voices East Asia
